sections.title: Provision resources when needed and adjust capacity to match demand
paragraphs: To run an application, you need servers to perform computing, storage for data, and a network for communication. If you buy the equipment yourself, you decide how many units you need and where to install them before use begins. If you have too little, you must wait for more equipment to arrive. If you have too much, you pay for equipment you do not use.

In the cloud, you can provision these resources over a network as needed. On-demand means requesting and using resources when they are needed. Instead of buying enough for the busiest period from the outset, you can start small and adjust capacity based on actual usage.

Scale out means increasing the number of units that share the workload; scale in means reducing that number. Scale up means increasing the capacity of a single unit. The ability to make a change is different from having it happen automatically, so if you want automatic adjustments, you must also set the conditions and limits.

With pay-as-you-go pricing, factors such as usage time, storage amount, and number of operations affect costs. Stopping compute resources you no longer use does not necessarily eliminate charges for disks or stored data you keep. Check what you use and retain for each resource.

example.scenario: We are moving an internal reporting workload to the cloud. It is small on weekdays, and usage increases only at the end of the month.
steps: Measure weekday requirements and avoid a setup that always runs the maximum number of units needed at month-end.
Increase compute resources to handle the month-end workload, then reduce them when it is finished.
Keep the data you still need after stopping compute, and check storage costs separately.
example.outcome: You can assess peak capacity and everyday costs separately. Usage must be monitored and adjusted.

misconception.claim: Moving to the cloud always lowers costs, even if you do nothing.
misconception.correction: Costs also increase when excess resources run, or when more data is stored or transferred. Measure what you need and review the design and usage.

takeaways: On-demand means resources can be used when needed.
Consider the ways to change capacity separately from the settings that automate those changes.
Check costs for each usage factor, such as computing and storage.

source.label: AWS: Six advantages of cloud computing

sections.title: What AWS manages and what you must protect
paragraphs: Using the cloud does not mean handing all security measures over to AWS. The Shared Responsibility Model provides a way to clarify the boundary between what AWS manages and what the user manages.

AWS manages the infrastructure that runs its services, including data center access and facilities. By contrast, decisions and settings such as who can access data, what data to store, and how much network traffic to allow are the user's responsibility.

The boundary varies by service. When you run an OS that you manage on EC2, you are responsible for updating that OS and any applications you install. With a service such as S3, where you do not directly operate the OS, AWS manages the underlying infrastructure, but you still manage settings such as who can access your data.

To determine who is responsible, first identify the service you are using, then identify the layer involved in the issue. Do not assume either that “it is on AWS, so AWS is responsible” or that “it involves data, so the user is responsible for everything.” Check who configures and operates each resource, and what they manage.

example.scenario: A Web application running on EC2 needs an OS update.
steps: Identify the target as the guest OS managed by the user, not AWS's physical server.
The user plans and applies the OS update, then verifies that it works.
At the same time, check for unnecessary network exposure and excessive application permissions.
example.outcome: Even when AWS protects the facilities, the user remains responsible for securing the OS and applications they manage.

misconception.claim: With a managed service, there are no security settings the user needs to check.
misconception.correction: Even when more layers of operation are handled for you, responsibilities such as managing data and access permissions remain with the user.

takeaways: Check the responsibility boundary for each service.
Distinguish the physical infrastructure from the user's settings and data.
The user is responsible for updating the EC2 guest OS.

sections.title: Separate failure domains with Regions and AZs
paragraphs: A Region is a geographic unit in which AWS resources are placed. Choose one by considering factors such as distance from users, required services, and constraints on where data may be stored. Simply switching the Region in the console does not move resources that have already been created.
An Availability Zone (AZ) is an isolated location within a Region. An AZ consists of one or more data centers. It is important not to think of an AZ and a Region as locations of the same scale.

Placing two servers in the same AZ may help protect against the failure of one server. However, an outage affecting that entire AZ can make both servers unavailable. Distributing workloads across different AZs separates this shared failure domain.

Placing resources in multiple AZs alone does not complete recovery for the entire system. Route connections from users to a functioning destination and make sure it can access the data it needs. Replicating to another Region also requires configuration and operation for the relevant service; all data is not automatically replicated around the world.

example.scenario: You run a website on two servers in the same AZ and want to prepare for an AZ failure.
steps: Check that the two current servers are in the same shared failure domain: an AZ.
Consider a design that also provides processing capacity in a different AZ and routes traffic to a healthy destination.
Check that the system can run using the remaining processing capacity and required data even if one AZ becomes unavailable.
example.outcome: Looking beyond server count to placement and dependencies lets you explain which failures a design is prepared for.

misconception.claim: If you increase the number to two servers, you can handle an AZ failure regardless of where they are placed.
misconception.correction: Two servers in the same AZ share the impact of an AZ failure. Check server count and failure domains separately.

takeaways: A Region contains multiple AZs.
Using multiple AZs helps separate the impact of a single AZ failure.
Check traffic routing and data dependencies as well as resource placement.

sections.title: Design around why downtime is unacceptable and the budget available
paragraphs: Availability is the property of a service being usable when needed. The same configuration is not suitable for every system. Start by clarifying who is affected if it stops, how long they can wait, and what kinds of failures the system should withstand.

For example, the impact of downtime differs between a temporary learning environment and a system that takes orders during business hours. For the latter, consider multiple processing targets and failover, while also accounting for the added cost and management burden of more resources and operations.

Distinguish increased load from a failure. Adding processing capacity can help handle congestion, but if all the added resources are within the same failure domain, protection against a failure in that location is still inadequate. Adjusting capacity and spreading placement serve different purposes.

When comparing designs, put into words what each prevents, what risks remain, and whether it can be operated within the available budget. For example, with three instances in AZ-a, all three stop during an AZ-a failure. With one instance each in AZ-a and AZ-b, one instance in AZ-b remains after an AZ-a failure. However, separately check whether that remaining instance can handle the required workload. Understanding residual risks, not just knowing cloud feature names, provides the foundation for choosing services in the next unit.

example.scenario: Compare two options. Option A has three instances in the same AZ; Option B has two instances in different AZs.
steps: Measure the required workload instead of judging performance by instance count alone.
If the goal is to withstand an AZ failure, check which shared failure modes Option B's placement reduces.
For Option B, also check the remaining instance's processing capacity, connection failover, and access to the data needed.
example.outcome: This lets you compare performance, failure domains, and operating costs separately instead of stopping at “more instances means safer.”

misconception.claim: Using multiple AZs eliminates the need to address load or check costs.
misconception.correction: AZ distribution provides protection against failure domains. Check remaining capacity and costs separately.

takeaways: Consider the required availability based on the impact of being unable to use the service.
Do not confuse capacity adjustment with distribution across failure domains.
Explain the remaining risks and operating burden as well as the benefits.

units.title: Core AWS Services
units.summary: Choose compute, storage, database, and execution models based on requirements.
units.objective: You can select AWS services based on execution, storage, and data characteristics.
explanation: Choose based on who manages the runtime environment, what you store, and how you search—not on the service name.
units.example: For image uploads, store images in S3 and choose EC2 or Lambda to run the transformation.

learningObjectives.text: Choose between EC2 and Lambda based on how much you want to manage the runtime environment and what triggers execution.
Choose between S3 and EBS based on the form of the data to be stored and what it needs to connect to.
Choose between RDS and DynamoDB based on how you query the data and your operational responsibilities.
Can separate requirements into compute, storage, and data roles, and explain how they fit together.

sections.title: Compute: Who manages the execution environment?
paragraphs: Compute services provide a place to run programs. Amazon EC2 instances are virtual servers where users choose the OS and manage applications and updates. EC2 is an option when you need detailed control over the OS or long-running processes.

AWS Lambda is a service that runs code in response to events. If you want to run a small task when a file arrives or an API is called, you provide a function and execution permissions instead of deciding on a fixed number of servers to keep running.

The decision is not simply “Do I need a server?” Check execution duration, OS dependencies, processes that run continuously, and what triggers execution, in that order. Compare EC2 first when you need OS configuration or long-running processes, and Lambda for event-based tasks.

example.scenario: I want to resize only the images that are uploaded.
steps: Put the image in S3.
Invoke Lambda on an object creation event.
Save the converted result under a different S3 key.
example.outcome: Lambda is a natural fit for this requirement because it processes only images as they arrive, without requiring you to manage a server that runs continuously.

misconception.claim: Lambda is always a higher-performance virtual server than EC2.
misconception.correction: Lambda is an event-driven code execution model. It is not a virtual server where you can freely manage the OS or continuously running services.

takeaways: EC2 is a virtual server where users manage the OS and applications.
Lambda runs code in response to events.
Choose based on what triggers execution and how much you need to manage.

sections.title: Storage: Objects or attached disks
paragraphs: Amazon S3 is object storage. Within a bucket, it handles objects such as files and images using keys. Applications use APIs to retrieve and store objects; it is not intended to be mounted directly as an OS directory.
Amazon EBS is block storage that you attach to an EC2 instance. Use it when you need storage that a virtual server reads and writes continuously, such as an OS file system or a database disk.

First, identify who uses the data. If multiple users retrieve files by key, use S3; if a specific EC2 instance's OS uses the storage as a disk, use EBS. Do not assume that storage and compute are the same service.

example.scenario: You want to store the OS disk for an application on EC2 and PDFs uploaded by users.
steps: Attach EBS for the OS and the application's file system.
Store PDFs as objects in an S3 bucket.
Specify the PDF to read using its S3 key.
example.outcome: By separating attached disks from shared files, you can choose a storage method that fits how the data is used.

misconception.claim: S3 is a disk attached to an EC2 instance.
misconception.correction: S3 is object storage accessed by key. EBS is what you attach to EC2 and use as a block device.

takeaways: S3 handles objects in a bucket by key.
EBS is block storage that you attach to EC2.
Choose based on how the data is used, not its storage format.

sections.title: Database: Queries and Operational Scope
paragraphs: Amazon RDS is a service for operating relational databases. When you want to work with business data using table relationships, SQL, and transactions, consider the database engine and connection settings.

Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database. You design access patterns around the table’s keys. Instead of assuming you can search arbitrary columns later, start by deciding which keys will be used to read and write data.

When choosing, do not stop at whether you can write SQL. Consider RDS when table joins and relationships are central, and DynamoDB when predictable key-based access with low operational overhead is the goal. Check the required queries and consistency against your requirements.

example.scenario: Link orders, order items, and customers, and run monthly aggregations.
steps: Organize the required table relationships and aggregations.
Check the requirements for joins and aggregations using SQL.
Consider RDS and design the engine, backups, and connections.
example.outcome: Because queries across relationships are central, RDS can be the starting point for comparison rather than a design that retrieves data using keys alone.

misconception.claim: DynamoDB can automatically run the same queries if you move RDS tables over unchanged.
misconception.correction: DynamoDB requires you to design the keys used for access first. Do not assume that it supports RDS-style join-centered queries unchanged.

takeaways: RDS works with relational tables and SQL.
DynamoDB uses access patterns designed around keys.
Narrow down candidates based on the queries you need.

source.label: Choosing between relational and nonrelational data stores

sections.title: Composition: Break requirements into roles
paragraphs: A single feature usually combines compute, storage, and a database. Instead of choosing one service to do everything, break the work down into input, processing, persistence, and querying, in that order.

For example, in a photo-sharing service, the file itself can be stored in S3, conversions handled by Lambda, and post details kept in a database. Separating service boundaries makes it clear where to investigate when processing fails and which permissions to grant.

The decision process is not about picking nouns out of the requirements. First describe in sentences who processes what and when, and how data will be stored and queried; then match each role to an appropriate service.

example.scenario: When a user submits a CSV, validate it, register the order information, and retain the original file.
steps: Store the original CSV in S3.
Use an arrival event to invoke Lambda and validate the format.
Register valid order information in a database suited to the required query pattern.
example.outcome: Separating files, event processing, and business data lets you review each responsibility independently when requirements change.

misconception.claim: If you choose EC2, you should design file storage and business data using EC2 alone.
misconception.correction: EC2 is a compute option. Choose S3 or a database separately to meet storage and query requirements.

takeaways: Break requirements down into compute, storage, and querying.
Choose services for each role.
Combining services clarifies boundaries between responsibilities and permissions.

units.title: Authentication and Authorization
units.summary: Distinguish identity verification, permissions, roles, and least privilege.
units.objective: Distinguish authentication, authorization, IAM roles, and least privilege when evaluating configurations.
explanation: Access control separates authentication, which verifies who someone is, from authorization, which determines what they are allowed to do.
units.example: Give people sign-in access, and give applications temporary permissions through roles.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish authentication from authorization and explain which stage failed.
Can explain how IAM principals and roles obtain temporary permissions.
Distinguish between policy allows and explicit denies.
Design access using least privilege and temporary credentials.

sections.title: Authentication and authorization answer different questions
paragraphs: Authentication verifies who the principal trying to access something is. Passwords, multi-factor authentication, and federation are ways to verify a person or principal.
Authorization determines which actions a verified principal is allowed to perform. If you can sign in but cannot read an S3 object, the request is being blocked by authorization after authentication.

When troubleshooting a failure, first check whether authentication succeeded, then check whether access is allowed to the target resource and action. Do not treat “can’t sign in” and “access denied” as the same problem.

example.scenario: A user can sign in to the console but cannot open the billing bucket.
steps: Confirm that a successful sign-in means authentication succeeded.
Check the requested S3 action and the target bucket.
Check the policy that allows or denies that action.
example.outcome: Because the user’s identity has been verified, investigate this as an authorization issue.

misconception.claim: If sign-in succeeds, you can operate on every AWS resource.
misconception.correction: Signing in is authentication. Separate policies authorize actual operations.

takeaways: Authentication verifies the principal.
Authorization grants permission to perform an action.
Check each stage in order to identify where the failure occurred.

sections.title: Principal and role: Who becomes what, temporarily
paragraphs: A principal is an entity that can perform actions in AWS. IAM users, roles, AWS services, and federated users can all be principals.

An IAM role is an identity with permission policies. An entity that assumes a role uses the permissions defined for that role as temporary credentials. The role itself has no long-term password or long-term access keys.

When granting permissions to an application, first design which principal will assume which role, before embedding access keys in a file. Assigning roles according to function helps limit permissions to the necessary duration and scope.

example.scenario: An application on EC2 saves output to a specific bucket.
steps: List only the S3 operations the application needs.
Create an IAM role with those permissions.
Associate the role with EC2, and have the application use temporary credentials.
example.outcome: Permissions can be tied to the role of the runtime environment without placing long-term access keys in the application configuration.

misconception.claim: A role is a container for storing a person's login password.
misconception.correction: A role is an identity with permissions that can be assumed. It has no long-term password or access keys.

takeaways: A principal is an entity that performs actions.
A role is an identity assumed to use its permissions.
A role uses temporary credentials.

sections.title: Policy: Check Deny as well as Allow
paragraphs: IAM policies define the actions a principal can perform on resources. When investigating, read specifically who is allowed to perform which actions on which resources.

Finding one Allow is not enough to reach a conclusion. In IAM evaluation, an explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow. Therefore, check for applicable denials in boundary policies, organization policies, resource-based policies, and so on.

To investigate AccessDenied, pin down the request’s principal, action, and resource; check the relevant Allow; then look for explicit Deny statements and conditions. Do not infer the cause from the displayed service name alone.

example.scenario: AccessDenied occurs for only one particular bucket despite having a read Allow.
steps: Identify the principal, s3:GetObject, and the key in the target bucket.
Check whether the Allow policy includes the target resource.
Check for explicit Deny statements and conditions in the bucket policy and other applicable policies.
example.outcome: By checking applicable Deny statements instead of relying only on whether an Allow exists, you avoid misidentifying the reason for the denial.

misconception.claim: If there is one Allow, you do not need to look at other policies.
misconception.correction: An explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow. Conditions and denials are also part of the evaluation.

takeaways: Policies link a subject, an action, and a resource.
An explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow.
Investigate by specifying the request precisely.

sections.title: Least Privilege and Temporary Credentials
paragraphs: Least privilege means allowing only the actions, resources, and conditions required for the job. Instead of starting with administrator permissions across all resources, observe the required operations and narrow the scope.
Temporary credentials are generated dynamically and have an expiration time. They can be used with roles and federation, helping reduce the risks of distributing and storing long-term access keys.

In implementation, do not share the same credentials among people, CI, and running applications. Use separate roles for each principal, and grant access only after checking the duration, target resources, and required actions.

example.scenario: Grant permissions to a job that only imports CSV files daily.
steps: List the input bucket to read from, the output bucket to write to, and the required operations.
Create a role policy limited to those operations and paths.
Associate the role with the job, and regularly review its actual usage.
example.outcome: You can avoid granting unnecessary deletion permissions or access to other buckets, while also limiting the impact if credentials are exposed.

misconception.claim: Least privilege means having only one user.
misconception.correction: It means granting each principal only the operations and targets it needs, regardless of the number of principals.

takeaways: Specify the required operations and targets.
Use temporary credentials with roles.
Separate permissions by principal.

choices.text: Because authentication has been strengthened, policies for the target resources are no longer needed.

choices.explanation: Attach permission policies to a role.

choices.text: AWS services can assume a role.
choices.explanation: Services such as EC2 can also use roles.

choices.explanation: Grant only the minimum permissions required to the role of the runtime environment.

choices.text: The application uses temporary credentials from the role.

choices.text: Write a long-term access key directly into the source code.

questions.title: Choosing a principal
questions.prompt: Select one incorrect statement about principals and roles.

choices.text: Principals exist only for people using the console; applications running on EC2 have no actor.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. A principal is an entity that performs an action, and is not limited to people. Even for a request in which an application on EC2 uses a role's temporary credentials, authorization checks which principal is making the request.

choices.text: Grant permissions only after identifying which principal will perform the action.
choices.explanation: Identifying the principal is the starting point.

choices.text: Do not share the same long-term key between a person and a running application.
choices.explanation: You can assign separate roles to each principal and use temporary credentials.

learning.reason: Both people and running applications have principals; match each with appropriate credentials and permissions.
learning.concept: A principal is not limited to a person.

questions.title: Explicit Deny
questions.prompt: Choose two statements that are correct about IAM policy evaluation.

choices.text: An explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow.
choices.explanation: An explicit deny takes precedence during evaluation.

choices.text: Once you find one Allow, you do not need to check any other policies.
choices.explanation: Check Deny statements and conditions as well.

choices.text: Policies are unrelated to resources.
choices.explanation: Evaluate by specifying the action and resource.

choices.text: When investigating, specify the principal, action, and resource.
choices.explanation: Evaluate the request with its details fixed.

choices.text: Deny applies only to encryption.
choices.explanation: Deny is part of access permission evaluation.

learning.reason: Understand the evaluation order.
learning.concept: An explicit Deny takes precedence.

questions.title: Investigating AccessDenied
questions.prompt: A read is denied even though there is an Allow. Select 2 correct investigation steps.

choices.text: Grant administrator permissions without checking what the error concerns.
choices.explanation: This violates least privilege and does not reveal the cause.

choices.text: Check whether the requested action and resource match the Allow.
choices.explanation: This checks for a mismatch in the target.

choices.text: Delete and recreate S3.
choices.explanation: This does not investigate policy evaluation.

choices.text: Ignore Deny if the request is authenticated.
choices.explanation: An explicit Deny takes precedence.

choices.text: Check for an explicit Deny and conditions in the bucket policy and other policies.
choices.explanation: These can cause a denial even when there is an Allow.

learning.reason: Check both permissions and denials.
learning.concept: Investigate by specifying the target precisely.

questions.title: Permission outcome
questions.prompt: Both an Allow for S3:GetObject and an explicit Deny for the same target are present. Choose 2 correct judgments.

choices.text: The operation is denied.
choices.explanation: An explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow.

choices.text: It will always succeed because there is an Allow.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect because it ignores the Deny.

choices.text: Investigate the policy and conditions that cause the Deny.
choices.explanation: This is the next step to narrow down the cause.

choices.text: The Deny will disappear if you authenticate again.
choices.explanation: Repeating authentication does not remove a policy Deny.

choices.text: S3 does not evaluate policies.
choices.explanation: Access is evaluated through IAM and resource policies, among other mechanisms.

learning.reason: Apply precedence rules when there is a conflict.
learning.concept: Deny takes precedence.

questions.title: Least privilege
questions.prompt: Select the 2 statements that are incorrect about least privilege.

choices.text: Specify the required actions and resources.
choices.explanation: This is the starting point for narrowing the scope of access.

choices.text: To make things work, grant administrator permissions for all resources from the outset.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. First determine the required scope.

choices.text: Separate the required roles for each principal.

choices.explanation: This helps determine how to reduce excessive permissions.

choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Limit permissions to the reads and writes that are needed.

choices.explanation: You can specify the resources precisely.

choices.text: Give the job role only the operations it needs.
choices.explanation: This follows the principle of least privilege for the principal.

choices.text: Consider a role that can use temporary credentials.
choices.explanation: This can reduce the distribution of long-term keys.

choices.text: Copy a developer’s personal access key into the job configuration.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Separate personal credentials from the execution environment.

learning.reason: Narrow the scope to what the job requires.
learning.concept: Use roles and temporary security credentials.

questions.title: Permission Design Sequence
questions.prompt: Select two statements that are incorrect as approaches to designing permissions for a new process.

choices.text: List the actions the process performs and the resources they target.
choices.explanation: This is a prerequisite for least privilege.

choices.text: Assign separate roles to each execution principal.
choices.explanation: This clarifies permission boundaries.

choices.text: Allow all actions to avoid troubleshooting failures.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. It expands the scope of impact.

choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Consider temporary credentials.

units.title: Data Protection
units.summary: Treat encryption, keys, recovery, and sensitive information as separate responsibilities.
units.objective: Assess protection at rest and in transit, key permissions, recovery, and the handling of secrets.
explanation: Design for recoverability and operations that do not expose secrets, as well as confidentiality.
units.example: Protect communications with TLS, encrypt data at rest with a KMS key, and test recovery.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish the purposes of encryption in transit and encryption at rest.
Explain KMS keys and permissions to use them.
Backup and actual restore testing can be designed separately.
Secrets can be separated from code and logs, and access permissions can be minimized.

sections.title: In Transit and At Rest: They Protect Different Stages
paragraphs: Encryption in transit helps prevent third parties from reading or tampering with data as it moves between a client and a service. HTTPS protects HTTP with TLS.
Encryption at rest protects data stored on disks, in databases, or as objects. Using TLS for communications does not automatically mean the destination encrypts stored data.

In a design, list data paths and storage locations separately. Check TLS for the paths from the browser to the API and from the API to the storage destination, and check the corresponding encryption settings at the destination.

example.scenario: A customer uploads a document through a web interface.
steps: Use HTTPS for communication between the browser and the API.
Also check that communication from the API to the storage service is encrypted.
Configure encryption at rest for the stored document.
example.outcome: This addresses two distinct situations: eavesdropping on communications and unauthorized access to storage media.

misconception.claim: HTTPS automatically encrypts data that has been stored.
misconception.correction: HTTPS protects data in transit. Check encryption at rest separately on the storage service side.

takeaways: Protect communication paths while data is in transit.
Protect stored data while it is at rest.
Check paths and storage destinations separately.

sections.title: KMS: The key itself and permission to use it
paragraphs: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) creates and manages encryption keys and supports encryption operations for AWS services and applications. It does more than enable encryption: it determines which key to use.

Access control for keys is important in KMS. A principal may be able to access data but still be unable to decrypt it if it is not permitted to perform the KMS operations required for decryption. Check the key policy and IAM permissions.
Secrets in Secrets Manager are encrypted with KMS at rest. Therefore, when troubleshooting, check permission to read the secret separately from permission to use the KMS key.

example.scenario: An application was denied when it tried to retrieve a database password from Secrets Manager.
steps: Identify the secret to retrieve and the execution role.
Check the permission to read from Secrets Manager.
Also check the permissions required to use the KMS key used for encryption.
example.outcome: By separating permission to access the secret itself from permission to use the key, you can pinpoint where the denial occurs.

misconception.claim: If you specify a KMS key, anyone can decrypt.
misconception.correction: The principal using the key must be authorized. The mere existence of a key does not grant permission to decrypt.

takeaways: KMS manages encryption keys.
Check data access permissions separately from key-use permissions.
Check the key policy and IAM permissions.

sections.title: Backup and recovery: Creating a backup and being able to restore are different
paragraphs: A backup preserves data or resources from a point in time for recovery. However, a successful backup job alone does not prove that you can restore them to the state you actually need.

For a restore, decide which recovery point to use, where to restore it, which steps to follow, and how to verify that the application is usable. AWS Backup restore testing is a way to assess recoverability regularly.

In your design, determine not only the retention period but also the recovery point objective, recovery time objective, and post-restore verification. Have a procedure for restoring to an isolated destination and checking the data and connections, rather than testing by overwriting production.

example.scenario: You operate nightly backups of order data.
steps: Choose the recovery point to use and an isolated restore destination.
Run restore jobs regularly.
Check the order count and application connections, and record the results.
example.outcome: You can verify not only that backups exist, but also that you can restore to a usable state within the required time.

misconception.claim: A notification that backup creation succeeded is enough to complete the recovery plan.
misconception.correction: You need to verify the restore procedure and post-restore usability in practice.

takeaways: Backup and restore verification are separate tasks.
Decide on the restore destination and verification criteria.
Check recoverability through regular tests.

sections.title: Secrets: Separate the value, its display, and who can retrieve it
paragraphs: Passwords, API keys, and tokens are secrets. Putting them in plaintext in source code, configuration files, chats, or logs increases the number of people who can view them and places where they are copied, and makes rotation harder.
AWS Secrets Manager stores secrets and encrypts them with KMS at rest. Let applications retrieve only the secrets they need through their execution roles.

Securely handling secrets takes more than providing a place to store them. Do not expose values in logs, limit which secrets are in scope, separate the principals that use them, and verify that consumers can keep up after updates.

example.scenario: An application uses a token for an external API.
steps: Remove the token from the source code and register it in Secrets Manager.
Allow the application execution role to retrieve only that secret.
Verify that the token value does not appear in logs or error messages.
example.outcome: This avoids exposing the token in repositories or logs and limits which principals can retrieve it.

misconception.claim: Environment variables make it safe to put secrets in logs.
misconception.correction: Regardless of how a secret is stored, displaying it in logs exposes it. Do not display the value, and narrow the retrieval scope.

takeaways: Separate secret values from code and logs.
Limit which principals can retrieve each secret.
Also check update and display paths.

choices.text: Protects data moving across a communication channel.

learning.concept: Distinguish data in transit from data at rest.

choices.text: It is a service for creating and managing encryption keys.
choices.explanation: KMS supports key management.

choices.text: If a key exists, every principal can use it unconditionally.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Permission to use the key is required.

choices.text: Data permissions and key usage permissions can be checked separately.

questions.title: Secret access denied

choices.text: Check only the secret read permission and do not check permissions for the KMS key.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Also check permissions to use the encryption key.

choices.text: Identify the application's execution role.
choices.explanation: Determine which principal made the request.

choices.text: Check the required permissions for both the secret and the KMS key.
choices.explanation: Both retrieval and decryption are involved.

learning.reason: Isolate where the access was denied.
learning.concept: Permissions for the secret and the key are separate.

questions.title: Separating key usage permissions
questions.prompt: When reading stored data fails, select the two correct investigation steps.

choices.text: Do not check permissions based only on the key name.
choices.explanation: You need to check permission to use the key.

choices.text: Identify the requesting principal and the KMS operation.
choices.explanation: Check who requested which key operation.

choices.text: Log the secret value to investigate.

units.title: Networking Fundamentals
units.summary: Diagnose IP, ports, TCP/UDP, and HTTP/TLS as stages of communication.
units.objective: Explain communication destinations, connection methods, and the stages at which applications or encryption can fail.
explanation: Troubleshoot communication in order: name resolution, IP routing, port, connection method, and application.
units.example: When you can’t connect over HTTPS, check DNS, IP routing, port 443, TLS, and HTTP in that order.

learningObjectives.text: Can distinguish the roles of an IP address and a port.
Can compare TCP and UDP in terms of connection orientation and reliability.
Distinguish the roles of HTTP and TLS.
Diagnose communication failures step by step.

sections.title: IP and port: Identifying a machine and a service
paragraphs: An IP address identifies the destination machine or network interface on a network. An IP address alone does not determine which service on that machine the traffic should reach.
A port is a number that distinguishes destination services on the same IP address. Clients connect to an IP address and port together, such as port 443, which a web server uses to receive HTTPS.

When a connection cannot be reached, check separately whether the name resolves to an IP address, whether there is a route to that IP address, and whether access to the destination port is permitted and a service is listening there. Knowing the IP address alone does not guarantee that the application can be reached.

example.scenario: You cannot connect to a web app from inside the company.
steps: Check the IP address returned by name resolution.
Check the route to that IP address.
Check that access to port 443 is permitted and that a service is listening.
example.outcome: You can investigate where the connection stops—at the destination, along the route, or at the service—without confusing the three.

misconception.claim: If you know the IP address, you can connect to any application.
misconception.correction: Ports distinguish services. Check both the IP address and the port.

takeaways: An IP address identifies the destination.
A port distinguishes services on the same IP address.
Check the route and port access separately.

source.label: IANA service names and port numbers

sections.title: TCP and UDP: Connection and Delivery Characteristics
paragraphs: TCP is a transport protocol that establishes a connection and handles ordering and delivery. It is used when lost data needs to be detected and handled in order, as in web communications.

UDP sends datagrams and does not provide connection establishment, retransmission, or ordering control as part of the protocol, as TCP does. For use cases that prioritize low latency, the application must consider any necessary controls.
Do not choose based only on “TCP is slow, UDP is fast.” Consider where ordering, retransmission, and connection management are handled, and which characteristics the use case requires.

example.scenario: Audio in a video conference has some packets that arrive late.
steps: Consider whether delayed, older audio still has value.
Check whether the communication method needs to handle ordering and retransmission.
Choose the method based on the use case’s tolerance for latency.
example.outcome: For use cases that prioritize current audio over fully retransmitting everything, UDP’s characteristics can be compared.

misconception.claim: UDP always delivers data in order.
misconception.correction: UDP does not provide ordering or retransmission guarantees like TCP does.

takeaways: TCP handles connection and reliability.
UDP does not provide connection establishment or retransmission.
Choose based on the delivery characteristics required.

sections.title: HTTP and TLS: The Meaning of Requests and Protecting the Communication Channel
paragraphs: HTTP is an application protocol that lets clients and servers exchange requests and responses. GET, POST, and status codes are part of HTTP’s semantics.

TLS is a protocol that provides authentication of communicating parties, confidentiality, and integrity. HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS; it does not define the meaning of HTTP URLs or responses themselves.

When troubleshooting, check in order whether the TCP connection can be established, whether the TLS handshake succeeds, and whether an HTTP response is returned. Do not handle certificate problems at the same stage as an HTTP 404.

example.scenario: Connecting to an https URL results in a certificate error.
steps: Check the name and IP address, and connectivity to port 443.
Check the TLS certificate and hostname.
Check the HTTP response after TLS is established.
example.outcome: This can be isolated as a problem at the TLS stage rather than an HTTP application error.

misconception.claim: TLS is the protocol that fixes HTTP 404 errors.
misconception.correction: TLS protects the communication channel. A 404 is an HTTP response indicating that a resource was not found.

takeaways: HTTP defines the meaning of requests and responses.
TLS protects the communication channel.
Distinguish TLS failures from HTTP failures.

sections.title: Troubleshooting: Fix the stages from the outside in
paragraphs: If you call a connectivity problem a “network failure” all at once, you cannot narrow down the cause. Separate, in order, the name used by the user, the DNS result, the IP path, port permissions such as those in a security group, TCP/UDP, TLS, and the HTTP response.

Fix the facts you observe at each stage. If DNS cannot resolve a name to an IP, it is not yet time to investigate ports or HTTP. If a TCP connection is refused, processing has not reached the HTTP application.

Align changes with a hypothesis about the cause. Before broadening port permissions, confirm the required destination and port and whether the service is listening; after the fix, repeat the observation at the same stage.

example.scenario: A user cannot connect to https://app.example.
steps: Verify that DNS resolves the name to the expected IP.
Verify that a connection can be made to the IP and port 443.
Check TLS, then the HTTP response.
example.outcome: By identifying the first stage that fails, you can avoid unnecessary application changes or overly broad network permissions.

misconception.claim: When there is no HTTP response, you should redeploy the application first.
misconception.correction: Check DNS, the path, ports, and TLS in order before investigating the stage that was reached.

takeaways: Separate the stages from the name through HTTP.
Identify the first point of failure.
After making changes, verify again using the same observation.

units.title: Domain Names and DNS
units.summary: Understand name resolution, records, TTL, and how DNS boundaries differ from HTTP/TLS.
units.objective: Explain DNS name resolution and records, describe the effects of TTL, and distinguish DNS from HTTP/TLS.
explanation: DNS maps names to information; it is not a web response or a certificate.
units.example: Lower the TTL before changing an IP, then check DNS results after the change while accounting for cache expiration.

learningObjectives.text: Can explain name resolution queries and the role of authoritative DNS.
Can distinguish the purposes of A, AAAA, CNAME, and NS records.
Can determine the relationship between TTL and how long it takes for changes to appear in the cache.
Can distinguish DNS, IP connectivity, TLS, and HTTP failures.

sections.title: Name resolution: From a name to the next question
paragraphs: DNS is a distributed system that maps human-readable names to IP addresses and other DNS information. Clients usually query a resolver for a name and, when needed, consult information from authoritative servers.
Authoritative DNS is the source of information that manages a zone’s records. When name resolution fails, check the queried name, delegation, NS records, and authoritative records in order.
Even if DNS returns an IP address, that does not guarantee that the web application is working. Name resolution comes before the connection; next, check the IP route, port, TLS, and HTTP.

example.scenario: app.example.com cannot be resolved.
steps: Check the complete name that was queried.
Check the zone’s NS delegation and authoritative records.
After receiving the expected response, check the IP connection.
example.outcome: You can separate name management issues from web application issues.

misconception.claim: If DNS returns an IP address, the web page will always be displayed.
misconception.correction: DNS only resolves names. The route, TLS, and HTTP must succeed separately.

takeaways: DNS maps names to information.
Authoritative DNS is the source of information for a zone.
Communication steps remain after resolution.

sections.title: Records: What They Map
paragraphs: An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address, while an AAAA record maps a name to an IPv6 address. Clients use them to obtain an IP destination.
A CNAME record treats a name as an alias for another name. The IP address of the final destination is obtained by resolving the alias target. A CNAME itself does not directly contain an IP address.

An NS record identifies the name servers that handle a zone. Distinguish A/AAAA, which direct IP traffic to a web service, CNAME, which creates an alias for a name, and NS, which identifies the delegation target, by their purpose.

example.scenario: You want to point www.example.com to a new host name.
steps: Check whether the connection target is a fixed IP address or another name.
If the requirement is to point to another name, consider a CNAME.
Handle NS only when you need to change the zone’s delegation target.
example.outcome: You can choose based on the information you want to map, rather than the record name.

misconception.claim: An NS record indicates the web server’s IPv4 address.
misconception.correction: NS identifies the name servers that handle a zone. An IPv4 address is represented by an A record.

takeaways: A is for IPv4; AAAA is for IPv6.
CNAME is an alias.
NS indicates the delegation target.

sections.title: TTL: How long cached information continues to be used
paragraphs: TTL is the number of seconds a DNS resolver can cache a record and use it without making another query. Even after you change a record, users with an existing cached copy may not see the new value right away.

A short TTL can help changes take effect sooner, but it increases the number of queries. A long TTL makes cached responses easier to use, but increases the time you may have to wait for changes to take effect.

If you plan to change an IP address, lower the TTL ahead of time rather than immediately before the change, and account for the expiration of the old TTL. After the change, check the expected value on both the authoritative side and the resolver side before restoring the TTL.

example.scenario: Change the website’s IP address tomorrow.
steps: Check the current TTL and how long you can wait before making the change.
Shorten the TTL in advance and wait for the old TTL to expire.
After changing the IP address, check the name resolution result and reset the TTL once it is stable.
example.outcome: Because the period during which cached data may remain is included in the schedule, propagation delays are less likely to be mistaken for an outage.

misconception.claim: The moment a DNS record is saved, caches for users around the world are cleared.
misconception.correction: Existing cached data remains valid until its TTL expires. Include the waiting period in your change plan.

takeaways: TTL is the amount of time data can be cached.
Short and long TTLs involve trade-offs.
Account for the old TTL before making a change.

sections.title: DNS is the entry point: HTTP and TLS have separate responsibilities
paragraphs: DNS resolves names to information such as IP addresses. TCP connections, TLS certificate validation, and HTTP responses happen after DNS, and each can fail for different reasons.
If name resolution fails, checking HTTP 404s or application logs first will not get you to the cause. Conversely, even if DNS is correct, HTTPS connections will fail if port 443 is closed.

During troubleshooting, distinguish observations of the name resolution response, IP/port connectivity, TLS, and HTTP response. Make changes only at the stage where the cause lies; do not mask a DNS problem with broad network permissions.

example.scenario: DNS returns the expected IP, but the browser reports a certificate error.
steps: Record that DNS succeeded.
Check the connection to port 443 and the hostname on the TLS certificate.
Check the HTTP response after TLS is established.
example.outcome: You can investigate the TLS stage without repeatedly changing DNS settings.

misconception.claim: A certificate error will always be fixed by changing the DNS record.
misconception.correction: Certificates are a TLS issue. Check them at the stage after DNS succeeds.

takeaways: DNS, connectivity, TLS, and HTTP are separate.
Identify the first stage that fails.
Make only changes that address the cause.

questions.title: IP change

choices.text: Shorten the TTL before the change and account for the expiration of the old TTL.

choices.text: Lowering the TTL at the same time as the change will clear existing caches.

choices.text: After the change, confirm that the expected resolution result is returned.

choices.text: Always keep the TTL set to the minimum.
choices.explanation: There is a trade-off with query volume.

choices.text: Use an HTTP 404 to confirm DNS propagation.
choices.explanation: Check the name resolution result.

choices.text: Check authoritative and resolver results separately.
choices.explanation: Find out where the old value remains.

choices.text: Open all ports.
choices.explanation: This is unrelated to DNS propagation.

choices.text: To fix a 404, change only the NS record.

choices.text: Check certificate errors at the TLS stage.
choices.explanation: This is after DNS.

questions.title: Certificate Error

choices.explanation: This checks the TLS stage.

choices.text: Changing the DNS record repeatedly will definitely fix it.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The problem occurs after DNS succeeds.

choices.explanation: Separate DNS from TLS.

choices.text: Waiting for HTTP 404 will make the certificate valid.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. A 404 does not fix a certificate problem.

learning.reason: Move on to the stage where the cause lies.
learning.concept: Certificates are part of TLS.

questions.title: Diagnosing Web Reachability
questions.prompt: Select the two incorrect steps in the sequence for diagnosing Web reachability.

choices.text: Check name resolution.
choices.explanation: This is the first step.

choices.text: Check the connection to the IP address and port.
choices.explanation: Check this after DNS.

choices.text: Investigate the application's 404 response even when DNS fails.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. HTTP has not been reached.

choices.text: Check TLS, then the HTTP response.
choices.explanation: Keep the stages separate.

choices.text: If the cause is unknown, delete all DNS records.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Make changes based on observations.

learning.concept: Proceed from DNS to HTTP.

units.title: CIDR and Subnets
units.summary: Determine the prefix, range, overlap, AWS-reserved IPs, and public access requirements.
units.objective: Read CIDR ranges, avoid overlap, and determine subnet reachability.
explanation: CIDR represents a network range using a prefix length, and AWS subnets have reserved IPs and routing requirements.
units.example: Divide 10.0.0.0/24 into non-overlapping /26 subnets, and check for a route to an IGW for public access.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the size of a range using an IPv4 CIDR block and its prefix length.
Can determine containment and overlap and divide subnets.
Can account for the reserved IP addresses in an AWS subnet.
Can determine whether a subnet is public or private by its routes, not its IP address.

sections.title: CIDR: The prefix length is the length of the network portion
paragraphs: CIDR represents IPv4 address ranges as 10.0.0.0/24, for example. In /24, the first 24 bits are the network portion, and the rest are the host portion. The larger the prefix, the smaller the range.
A /24 contains 256 IPv4 addresses, and a /26 contains 64. Instead of relying only on memorizing ranges, check that increasing the prefix by two makes the number of addresses one quarter as large.

When designing, decide on the overall VPC range first, then choose prefixes based on the number of subnets needed and room for future expansion. Subtract AWS-reserved IP addresses afterward to determine the number available.

example.scenario: Divide 10.0.0.0/24 into 4 ranges.
steps: Divide the 256 addresses in /24 into 4 equal parts.
Lay out each range as a /26 with 64 addresses.
Check the boundaries, such as 10.0.0.0/26 and 10.0.0.64/26.
example.outcome: You can explain how to divide a range without overlaps by understanding the relationship between the prefix and the range.

misconception.claim: A /26 represents a larger range than a /24.
misconception.correction: A /26 has a larger prefix and fewer host bits, so it represents a smaller range.

takeaways: The larger the prefix, the smaller the range.
A /24 has 256 addresses; a /26 has 64.
Consider room for future expansion when designing.

sections.title: Partitioning: Check containment and overlap first
paragraphs: Subnets must be within the VPC CIDR and must not overlap one another. Within 10.0.0.0/24, 10.0.0.0/25 and 10.0.0.128/25 are adjacent and do not overlap.
10.0.0.0/25 and 10.0.0.64/26 overlap. The latter is contained within the former, so they cannot both be allocated as separate subnets.

Before creating a subnet, write down its start and end addresses and check that it fits within the VPC and does not intersect any existing range. Different names or AZs do not eliminate IP range overlap.

example.scenario: Add a new subnet to the existing 10.0.0.0/25.
steps: Confirm that the existing range ends at 10.0.0.127.
Set the new candidate to 10.0.0.128/25.
Also confirm that it is contained within the VPC CIDR.
example.outcome: Because it uses an adjacent range, it does not overlap the existing subnet.

misconception.claim: You can use the same CIDR for two subnets if they are in different AZs.
misconception.correction: Subnet CIDRs within a VPC cannot overlap, regardless of AZ.

takeaways: Subnets are contained within the VPC.
Check for overlap using the start and end addresses.
AZ names do not resolve CIDR overlap.

sections.title: AWS Reserved IP Addresses: Not All Addresses Are Usable
paragraphs: In AWS IPv4 subnets, the first 4 and the last IP address cannot be assigned to resources. In a /24, 5 of the 256 addresses are reserved.
For example, in 10.0.0.0/24, AWS reserves .0 for the network, .1 for the VPC router, .2 for DNS, .3 for future use, and .255 as the network broadcast address.

If you count only the number of EC2 instances you need and choose the smallest range, you may run short. Add the 5 reserved addresses and room for growth to the required capacity, then choose an allowed CIDR range.

example.scenario: Place 50 resources in one subnet.
steps: Add the 5 reserved addresses to the 50 required addresses.
Determine that 32 addresses in a /27 are insufficient.
Subtract the 5 reserved addresses from the 64 in a /26 and confirm that 59 are usable.
example.outcome: A /26 can accommodate 50 resources and the reserved IP addresses.

misconception.claim: All 256 addresses in a /24 can be assigned to EC2.
misconception.correction: AWS reserves the first 4 addresses and the last 1.

takeaways: Reserve 5 addresses in each IPv4 subnet.
Add the reserved addresses to the required capacity.
Do not mechanically choose the smallest prefix.

sections.title: public/private: Determined by the route
paragraphs: In AWS, a subnet associated with a route table that has a route to an internet gateway is called a public subnet. A subnet’s name or CIDR numbers alone do not determine whether it is public.

To reach an instance over IPv4 from the internet, it needs a route to an IGW as well as a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP, for example. Creating the route alone does not necessarily expose every instance to the internet.

When designing a network, check why only the necessary entry points are placed in public subnets, while the application and data tiers are placed in private subnets. Check, in order, the route table association, the destination of 0.0.0.0/0, and the address on the instance.

example.scenario: Cannot connect from outside to an EC2 instance in a subnet named public.
steps: Check whether the subnet’s route table has a route to an IGW.
Check whether the EC2 instance has a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP.
Check that the required port is allowed and that the service is listening.
example.outcome: You can diagnose reachability from routes and addresses, not names.

misconception.claim: A subnet with CIDR 10.0.0.0/24 is automatically a public subnet.
misconception.correction: Whether a subnet is public is determined by its association with a route table that has a route to an IGW.

takeaways: Determine public/private status from the route table.
External IPv4 reachability requires a route and a public IP.
Do not judge by the name or CIDR alone.

That divides it into 4 equal parts of 64 each.

choices.explanation: It is 2 to the 8th power.

choices.text: A /26 contains 64 IPv4 addresses.

choices.explanation: Two /26 ranges contain 128 addresses in total, which is not enough for a /24 with 256 addresses. When they are contiguous and aligned to a /25 boundary, as with 10.0.0.0/26 and 10.0.0.64/26, they can be combined into one /25.

learning.reason: Apply the relationship between ranges.
learning.concept: A /24 consists of four /26 ranges.

questions.title: Overlap
questions.prompt: Choose one incorrect statement about subnet design.

choices.text: Place subnets within the VPC CIDR.
choices.explanation: Check containment.

choices.text: The same CIDR can be used if the subnets are in different AZs.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. CIDRs cannot overlap within a VPC.

choices.text: Check for overlap using the start and end addresses.
choices.explanation: You can compare the ranges.

learning.reason: Prevent overlap.
learning.concept: AZs do not allow overlap.

questions.title: Adjacent ranges
questions.prompt: With an existing 10.0.0.0/25, select the one option that is incorrect as a new subnet candidate.

choices.explanation: 10.0.0.64–10.0.0.127 falls within the existing /25 range and overlaps it, so it cannot be added.
10.0.0.128–10.0.0.191 is outside the existing /25 range and does not overlap.
10.0.0.192–10.0.0.255 is outside the existing /25 range and does not overlap.

learning.reason: The existing 10.0.0.0/25 covers 10.0.0.0 through 10.0.0.127. Compare both the start and end of each candidate range.
learning.concept: Assign CIDR blocks that do not overlap the existing range to other subnets.

questions.title: Design check
questions.prompt: Before adding a new CIDR to an existing subnet, select the one condition that must be met first.

choices.text: Confirm that the proposed range is within the VPC CIDR and does not overlap any existing range.
choices.explanation: A subnet must be contained within the VPC and must not overlap any existing subnet in the VPC.

choices.text: If the AZ names differ, there is no need to check CIDR ranges.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. CIDRs within a VPC cannot overlap, regardless of AZ.

choices.text: Checking only the starting address is enough; there is no need to check the ending address.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Check both the start and end of each range to determine whether the ranges overlap.

choices.text: A subnet can be added even if it is contained within an existing range, as long as its name is different.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. A different name does not resolve CIDR overlap.

choices.text: CIDR overlap is allowed if you use separate route tables.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Routing configuration does not resolve overlapping CIDRs.

learning.reason: Check containment and non-overlap first.
learning.concept: Subnets must be within the VPC and must not overlap.

questions.title: Reserved IP addresses
questions.prompt: Select the two correct statements about AWS IPv4 subnets.

choices.text: All IP addresses can be assigned to EC2 instances.
choices.explanation: Five IP addresses are reserved.

choices.text: The first four and the last IP addresses are reserved.
choices.explanation: These are AWS-reserved IP addresses.

choices.text: The number of reserved addresses is determined by the port number.
choices.explanation: The reservation applies within the CIDR block.

choices.text: In a /24 subnet, .255 can be assigned.
choices.explanation: The last IP address is reserved.

choices.text: Include reserved IP addresses when estimating the number of instances needed.
choices.explanation: This lets you calculate the number of available addresses correctly.

learning.reason: Avoid miscalculating the number of available addresses.
learning.concept: Five IP addresses are reserved in each subnet.

questions.title: 50 hosts
questions.prompt: Choose two correct approaches to subnet sizing for 50 hosts.

choices.text: A /27 has 32 addresses, so it is insufficient.
choices.explanation: It falls short of 50 even before reservations.

choices.text: Assume all 64 addresses in a /26 can be assigned.
choices.explanation: 5 addresses are reserved.

choices.text: A /26 provides 59 usable addresses, enough for 50 hosts.
choices.explanation: 64 − 5 = 59 addresses.

choices.text: Reserved IP addresses are needed only during communication, so there is no need to account for them in planning.
choices.explanation: They cannot be assigned, so include them in your planning.

choices.text: Choose based only on the number of hosts without considering CIDR.
choices.explanation: Check the address range and reservations.

learning.reason: Include reservations in your calculation.
learning.concept: A /26 has 59 usable addresses.

questions.title: Reserved IPs and their impact
questions.prompt: Select two correct statements about how reserved IPs are handled.

choices.text: Use a reserved IP for an EC2 instance when addresses are scarce.
choices.explanation: Reserved IPs cannot be assigned.

choices.text: Choose a range that also allows room for future growth.
choices.explanation: This helps avoid running out of addresses.

choices.text: Reserved IPs are relevant only to S3.
choices.explanation: These are IP addresses in a VPC subnet.

choices.text: Estimate by adding the number of required instances and reserved addresses.
choices.explanation: This gives you an accurate view of the number available.

choices.text: If the prefix is the same, you can ignore reserved addresses.
choices.explanation: Always subtract reserved addresses.

learning.reason: Account for reserved addresses in your plan.

questions.title: public subnet
questions.prompt: Select two statements about a public subnet that are incorrect.

choices.text: A subnet with CIDR 10.0.0.0/24 is automatically public.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Its route determines whether it is public.

choices.text: Check its association with a route table that has a route to an IGW.
choices.explanation: This is the criterion for determining whether a subnet is public.

choices.text: To reach external IPv4 addresses, also check for a public IP address.
choices.explanation: A route alone is not sufficient.

choices.text: Check the route table, not just the subnet name.
choices.explanation: The name is not a criterion for determining whether a subnet is public.

choices.text: If a subnet is named private, it is private even if it has a route to an IGW.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The route determines whether it is public.

learning.reason: Do not judge by the name.
learning.concept: A public subnet has a route to an IGW.

questions.title: External connectivity
questions.prompt: EC2 cannot be reached from outside. Select 2 incorrect troubleshooting steps.

choices.text: Check the route table for a route to the IGW.
choices.explanation: This is a routing requirement.

choices.text: Do not check the route because the subnet is named public.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The name is not a basis for judgment.

choices.text: Check the EC2 instance's public IPv4 address or Elastic IP.
choices.explanation: This is an IPv4 reachability requirement.

choices.text: Look only at the CIDR and do not check port permissions or listening services.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The later stages of communication also need to be checked.

choices.text: Check that access is allowed to the required port.
choices.explanation: This is a connection requirement.

learning.reason: Check multiple reachability requirements.
learning.concept: A route, an IP address, and a port are required.

questions.title: Designing public access
questions.prompt: Select two statements that are incorrect as a design for determining public accessibility.

choices.text: Check why only necessary entry points are placed in a public subnet.
choices.explanation: This limits the scope of public access.

choices.text: Check the route table associations.
choices.explanation: This helps determine the routing.

choices.text: Determine reachability based only on the CIDR numbers.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Both the route and the address are needed.

choices.text: Design external connectivity requirements for the private tier separately.
choices.explanation: Consider requirements other than direct connectivity to an IGW.

choices.text: If there is a route to an IGW, a security group is unnecessary.

learning.concept: Public accessibility depends on multiple conditions.

units.title: Routing and connectivity
units.summary: Troubleshoot communication failures by checking the destination, route, exposure scope, and filters in order.
units.objective: Explain and investigate communication within and outside a VPC by separating routes from control points.
explanation: Select the most specific route for the destination, then check reachability through that route and whether the communication is allowed.
units.example: When updates fail in a private subnet, check the route to the NAT, the NAT's placement, and return traffic, in that order.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the role of a route based on its destination CIDR and target.
Distinguish the uses and requirements of an IGW and a NAT gateway.
Distinguish the statefulness and scope of security groups and network ACLs.
Trace the private connection path by checking the name, route, and permission, in that order.

sections.title: A route determines the next destination for each address
paragraphs: A VPC route table maps destination CIDRs to targets for packets leaving a subnet. Once the destination IP is known, the route containing that IP is selected.

The local route keeps traffic for CIDRs within the VPC. When multiple routes in the same table match a destination IP, the longest prefix—that is, the most specific CIDR—is selected. For example, 10.1.2.3 matches both 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.0.0/16, so 10.1.0.0/16 is selected. Don’t decide by looking only at the default route; check how the CIDRs overlap.
Even if a route exists, its target may not reach the other side. Routes on the target side, VPN or peering configuration, and the return path are also required.

example.scenario: An EC2 instance in 10.0.2.0/24 cannot connect to 10.1.0.10.
steps: Find the route in the subnet’s table that contains destination 10.1.0.10.
If the target is peering, check whether the other VPC also has a return route to 10.0.2.0/24.
After checking the route, verify that communication is allowed on both sides.
example.outcome: You can explain separately whether the missing piece is the destination route, the outbound path, or the return path.

misconception.claim: If 0.0.0.0/0 exists, all private networks are reachable.
misconception.correction: The target of the default route may not know how to reach that private network. You need a target matching the destination and routes in both directions.

takeaways: A route is a pair of a destination CIDR and a target.
Check reachability in both directions, including the return path.

sections.title: IGW enables public reachability; NAT supports outbound traffic from private subnets
paragraphs: An Internet Gateway (IGW) attaches to a VPC and serves as a target for internet-bound routes in a route table. For an EC2 instance to be reachable from outside over IPv4, it needs a route to the IGW and a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP.
A NAT gateway is used when resources in a private subnet need to initiate outbound IPv4 traffic. The NAT gateway itself must be placed in a public subnet, which needs a route to the IGW.

Placing a NAT gateway in a private subnet alone does not provide an exit to the internet. Check both steps: point the private subnet’s default route to the NAT gateway, and the default route in the NAT gateway’s subnet to the IGW. A NAT gateway does not respond to ping requests sent to its own IP address, so do not conclude there is a failure solely because ping gets no reply. Check that its status is Available, both routes are in place, and the traffic is allowed.

example.scenario: Allow only patch downloads from a private subnet; do not allow SSH from the internet.
steps: Place the EC2 instance in a private subnet without a public IPv4 address.
Point 0.0.0.0/0 in the private subnet to the NAT gateway.
Place the NAT gateway in a public subnet that has a route to the IGW and a public IPv4 address.
example.outcome: The EC2 instance can initiate outbound communication, while remaining isolated from direct inbound traffic through the IGW.

misconception.claim: Creating a NAT gateway automatically gives a private subnet access to the internet.
misconception.correction: Traffic will not flow without a route in the private subnet and a route from the NAT gateway’s subnet to the IGW.

takeaways: The IGW is a route target that enables public reachability.
NAT is an exit for IPv4 traffic initiated from the private side.

sections.title: Check the route first, then verify subnet and instance permissions
paragraphs: A Security Group is a stateful filter associated with an instance or network interface. Return traffic for an allowed connection is automatically allowed, so typically you allow only the required source and port.
A Network ACL is a stateless filter applied to a subnet. Because inbound and outbound traffic are evaluated separately, design both directions, including the ephemeral ports used for return traffic.

Routes, NACLs, and Security Groups are not alternatives. Routes handle destinations, NACLs handle the subnet boundary, and Security Groups handle the instance boundary, so check them in order along the traffic path.

example.scenario: HTTPS from the ALB to the Web EC2 instance is failing.
steps: Confirm that the local route from the ALB subnet to the EC2 subnet is present.
Allow port 443 from the ALB's Security Group in the EC2's Security Group.
If using a NACL, check the inbound and outbound rules required for traffic in both directions.
example.outcome: You can determine which direction to allow at which boundary, rather than simply opening a port.

misconception.claim: Allowing 443 in the Security Group makes the NACL outbound rule unnecessary.
misconception.correction: Because NACLs are stateless, the return direction must also be allowed separately.

takeaways: Security Groups are stateful and apply at the instance level.
NACLs are stateless and apply at the subnet level.

sections.title: Investigate private connections by separating names, routes, and permissions
paragraphs: Even when connecting to a private IP, first check the name resolution result. If the name returns an unintended public IP, inspecting routes or Security Groups afterward will not lead to the intended private path.

Next, check whether the source subnet's route sends the destination CIDR or prefix list to the correct target. VPC peering, Transit Gateway, VPN, and interface endpoints serve different purposes; simply connecting them does not provide automatic reachability to every CIDR.
Finally, check the NACLs, Security Groups, and the peer's return route. Fixing just one of DNS, routing, or authorization will not make communication succeed if another layer is missing.

example.scenario: The application cannot connect to a private endpoint for an AWS service.
steps: Check whether the destination name resolves to the endpoint's private IP.
Check the route from the subnet to the endpoint or the endpoint's usage requirements.
If the configuration uses an endpoint policy or Security Group, check whether the caller is permitted.
example.outcome: Instead of concluding that it is a “DNS failure,” you can troubleshoot names, reachability, and permissions in order.

misconception.claim: Peering VPCs automatically permits all traffic between them.
misconception.correction: Routes on both sides and permissions at each boundary are required; Security Groups and NACLs do not open automatically.

takeaways: Treat name resolution, routing, and permissions as separate checkpoints.
Private connections also require a return route and controls on the peer side.

questions.title: Route configuration
questions.prompt: Choose one correct statement about VPC routes.

choices.text: A route maps a destination CIDR or prefix list to a target.
choices.explanation: As described in the text, a route is a rule that determines the next destination based on the destination address.

choices.text: A route records only the inbound ports for a Security Group.
choices.explanation: Port permissions are handled by filters such as Security Groups; routes handle destinations and targets.

choices.text: A route always converts DNS names to public IP addresses.
choices.explanation: DNS converts names to IP addresses; this is not the role of a route table.

learning.reason: Distinguishing destinations from targets keeps troubleshooting routes separate from troubleshooting permissions.
learning.concept: Explain the role of a route using the destination CIDR and target.

questions.title: Peering return route
questions.prompt: You cannot connect from 10.0.2.0/24 to 10.1.0.10 over VPC peering. Select the one incorrect investigation step.

choices.text: Check the route and target for 10.1.0.10 in the source subnet.
choices.explanation: First, check that the source has a route to send traffic to the destination.

choices.text: Check whether the peer VPC has a return route to 10.0.2.0/24.
choices.explanation: The response must also be able to return to the source.

choices.text: If one side has a default route, do not check the route on the other side.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. With peering, reachable routes are required on both sides.

learning.reason: This prevents you from judging the connection successful based only on checking the outbound path.
learning.concept: For private communications, check the routes on both the source and peer sides.

questions.title: Reachability assessment
questions.prompt: Choose the two correct reasons why having a route alone does not guarantee successful communication.

choices.text: Without a return route on the other side, the response may not get back.
choices.explanation: Two-way communication also requires a return path.

choices.text: The route table needs to resolve DNS names.
choices.explanation: Name resolution is the responsibility of DNS; route tables handle IP destinations.

choices.text: If a route exists, NACLs and Security Groups are not evaluated.
choices.explanation: Routing and filtering are separate control points, and both affect communication.

choices.text: The target may lack the required connection configuration or reachability.
choices.explanation: Even if a target is selected, the configuration may not provide a path all the way to it.

choices.text: The local route must always be deleted before checking external communication.
choices.explanation: The local route is kept for communication within a VPC; deleting it is not the right course of action.

learning.reason: You need to check routing, connectivity, and permissions in sequence.
learning.concept: A route is one of the conditions necessary for communication to succeed.

questions.title: External reachability requirements
questions.prompt: Choose the two statements that are incorrect as requirements for making an EC2 instance reachable from the internet over IPv4.

choices.text: Add an internet-bound route with the IGW as its target to the subnet's route table.
choices.explanation: An IGW is a target for routes to the internet.

choices.text: Assign a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP to the EC2 instance.
choices.explanation: A public IPv4 address or Elastic IP is required for IPv4 communication through an IGW.

choices.text: A NAT gateway in the same private subnet makes an IGW unnecessary.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. A public NAT gateway is placed in a public subnet that has a route to an IGW.

choices.text: Allow the required traffic using security groups or similar controls.
choices.explanation: Separate from routing, you need settings that allow the traffic.

choices.text: A private IPv4 address alone lets the IGW automatically translate the address for external access.
