choices.explanation: This is incorrect. External reachability over IPv4 requires a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP.

learning.reason: Review the public subnet's route, address, and traffic permissions together.
learning.concept: Distinguish the purposes and requirements of an IGW and a NAT gateway.

questions.title: Purpose of NAT
questions.prompt: Choose one correct use of a NAT gateway.

choices.text: Allow SSH connections to be initiated directly from outside to an EC2 instance in a private subnet.
choices.explanation: NAT provides an egress path for traffic initiated from the private side; it is not intended for direct inbound connections.

choices.text: Provide an egress path for an EC2 instance in a private subnet without a public IPv4 address to retrieve updates from outside.
choices.explanation: As in the patch retrieval example in the lesson, it supports traffic initiated from the private side.

choices.text: Omit all Security Group rules in the VPC.
choices.explanation: NAT is not an authorization mechanism that replaces Security Groups or NACLs.

learning.reason: Distinguishing the direction in which a connection is initiated prevents the misconception that NAT is a way to expose services for inbound access.
learning.concept: NAT provides an egress path for IPv4 traffic initiated from the private side.

questions.title: Investigating NAT routing
questions.prompt: Patch retrieval failed from a private subnet. Select one investigation step that is incorrect.

choices.text: Check whether the private subnet’s default route targets the NAT gateway.
choices.explanation: A route from the source to the NAT is required.

choices.text: Check whether the NAT gateway is Available.
choices.explanation: It cannot function as an egress point unless it is available.

choices.text: Check whether the NAT’s public subnet has a route to the IGW.
choices.explanation: The NAT itself must be able to reach external networks.

choices.text: Conclude that the NAT is faulty if it cannot be pinged.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. NAT gateways do not respond to ping, so check their state, routes, and permissions.

learning.reason: This prevents concluding that a reachability symptom has a single cause based on just one test result.
learning.concept: Isolate NAT issues in this order: state, both route hops, and traffic permissions.

questions.title: Filter Differences
questions.prompt: Choose two correct statements about security groups and network ACLs.

choices.text: A security group is stateful and automatically allows return traffic for an allowed connection.
choices.explanation: Security groups track connection state.

choices.text: A network ACL is a stateful filter applied at the instance level.
choices.explanation: A NACL is a stateless filter applied at the subnet level.

choices.text: A network ACL allows inbound and outbound traffic separately for each direction of a connection.
choices.explanation: Because it is stateless, return traffic must also be handled explicitly.

choices.text: A security group defines only deny rules.
choices.explanation: Security groups are a mechanism for defining allow rules.

choices.text: If a route exists, the NACL is not evaluated.
choices.explanation: Routes, NACLs, and security groups are evaluated at different layers.

learning.reason: Separating scope from statefulness (stateful/stateless) helps determine which rules are needed.
learning.concept: Distinguish the state tracking and scope of security groups and network ACLs.

questions.title: NACL Return Traffic
questions.prompt: An HTTPS response from the ALB to the EC2 instance is not returning in a subnet that uses a NACL. Select the two incorrect judgments.

choices.text: Check return traffic in both the inbound and outbound directions of the NACL.
choices.explanation: NACLs are stateless, so rules are required in both directions.

choices.text: If the Security Group is stateful, an outbound rule in the NACL is unnecessary.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. NACLs are evaluated independently of Security Groups.

choices.text: Allow port 443 from the ALB's Security Group in the EC2 instance's Security Group.
choices.explanation: At the instance boundary, you can restrict the source to the ALB's Security Group.

choices.text: Do not check the ALB subnet because NACLs are associated only with EC2 instances.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. NACLs are applied to subnets, so check both subnets along the path.

choices.text: Treat routes and filters as separate inspection points.
choices.explanation: Routes determine the destination, while filters determine whether traffic is allowed.

learning.reason: To avoid incorrectly applying the stateful behavior of Security Groups to NACLs.
learning.concept: With NACLs, explicitly inspect the return direction as well.

questions.title: Layer-by-layer checks
questions.prompt: Choose the correct order for investigating communication.

choices.text: Open only the Security Group, then create a route if it fails.
choices.explanation: Before broadening permissions, also check the path to the destination.

choices.text: Delete the NACL, then check the destination.
choices.explanation: Inspect the route and each filter in sequence without removing controls.

choices.text: Check the route, the NACL at the subnet boundary, and the Security Group at the instance boundary, in that order.
choices.explanation: This investigation follows the control points described in the lesson.

learning.reason: You can identify the layer causing the issue and review the smallest necessary setting.
learning.concept: A route, NACL, and Security Group are separate control points, not substitutes for one another.

questions.title: Troubleshooting private connectivity
questions.prompt: Choose the one incorrect troubleshooting step when you cannot connect to a private endpoint.

choices.text: Check whether the destination name resolves to the intended private IP.
choices.explanation: If the name returns a different IP, traffic will not follow the intended path.

choices.text: If DNS succeeds, do not check routes or permissions.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Name resolution, reachability, and permissions are separate checkpoints.

choices.text: Check the route to the destination or the endpoint usage requirements.
choices.explanation: Even after name resolution, you still need to be able to reach the actual destination.

learning.reason: This helps avoid confusing successful DNS resolution with successful communication.
learning.concept: For private connectivity, investigate names, routes, and permissions separately.

questions.title: Checks after peering
questions.prompt: Select the two checks that are also required after creating VPC peering.

choices.text: Add a route to the other VPC’s CIDR to the route tables in both VPCs.
choices.explanation: Simply connecting the peering does not create routes from each subnet.

choices.text: The Security Groups and NACLs in both VPCs are automatically opened to all traffic.
choices.explanation: Allow rules are not changed automatically; define the required scope.

choices.text: DNS names always automatically return private IPs, so no checks are needed.
choices.explanation: Check that name resolution also points to the intended destination.

choices.text: No route is needed for return traffic.
choices.explanation: A return route is also required for two-way communication.

choices.text: Check that the Security Groups and NACLs allow the required communication.
choices.explanation: Even when a route exists, a connection cannot be made if a filter blocks the traffic.

learning.reason: Distinguish between a connection object and a usable network path.
learning.concept: For a private connection, check the routes and permissions on both sides.

questions.title: Troubleshooting hypotheses
questions.prompt: Name resolution returns a private IP, and the source route is correct, but the connection still fails. Select the 2 incorrect next steps.

choices.text: Check the peer’s return route.
choices.explanation: Without a route for the response to return, the connection cannot be established.

choices.text: Since name resolution is correct, the filters must be allowing the traffic.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. DNS and traffic authorization operate at different layers.

choices.text: Check permissions along the path, such as NACLs and Security Groups.
choices.explanation: After confirming reachability, check the permissions at each boundary.

choices.text: Open every Security Group to 0.0.0.0/0 to test.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Maintain least privilege even when troubleshooting.

choices.text: If the configuration uses a destination endpoint policy, check whether the caller is permitted.
choices.explanation: An endpoint-specific policy may be the cause of a denial.

learning.reason: Separate the layers already observed from those not yet verified to narrow down the cause safely.
learning.concept: Investigate private connectivity failures by testing hypotheses about names, routes, and permissions.

units.title: CI/CD Workflow
units.summary: Learn how to check changes and progressively deploy the same artifact.
units.objective: Explain why changes are checked and only verified artifacts are deployed safely.
explanation: Changes are integrated, then proceed through build, test, and deployment.
units.example: A failed check stops promotion and preserves the last known good version.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the purpose of CI as it progresses from commit to build and test.
Distinguish continuous delivery from continuous deployment, and understand the role of approvals.
Explain why an artifact is built once and the same artifact is promoted.
Determine the procedure for stopping failures with quality gates and staged promotion.

sections.title: CI is a process that takes in changes starting from a commit and automatically runs builds and tests. Integrating small changes frequently makes it easier to narrow down the cause of a problem.
paragraphs: A build creates a distributable artifact, and tests check for defects. A successful result does not guarantee production safety; it is a result that allows you to move to the next stage.

A pipeline may arrange stages called Source, Test, and Deploy. For example, Source passes changes along, Test checks them, and Deploy distributes them to the target environment. Stage names and how they are divided vary by tool and organization.
When a failure occurs, check the logs, make a fix, and rerun the same checks without proceeding to later stages.
A developer commits a small change.

example.scenario: Bring the commit into CI.
steps: Run the build and tests.
If they fail, investigate the cause without deploying.
You can stop a broken change early.
example.outcome: After CI succeeds, you can always deploy to production without approval.

misconception.claim: CI performs checks; approval and deployment methods are designed separately.
misconception.correction: A commit is the starting point for CI.

takeaways: Builds and tests are checks used to make decisions about later stages.
Fix failures and run the checks again.
AWS CodePipeline concepts מלא?

sections.title: Distinguishing delivery from deployment
paragraphs: Continuous delivery keeps tested changes in a state where they can be released at any time.
Continuous deployment automatically deploys changes that pass testing to production without approval.
Approval is not a substitute for testing; it is a checkpoint to review impact and the monitoring plan.

example.scenario: Deploying a tested web application to production.
steps: Keep the candidate release ready.
Review the impact and monitoring plan.
Deploy after approval.
example.outcome: You can distinguish a release-ready state from automatic deployment.

misconception.claim: Delivery and deployment are the same, and deployment always happens automatically.
misconception.correction: Delivery means being ready to release; deployment automates the process through production deployment.

takeaways: Delivery means the release-ready state.
Deployment proceeds through production deployment.
Approval is a separate decision point.

sections.title: Build an artifact once and promote it
paragraphs: An artifact is a package or container produced by a build. Rebuilding separately for each environment may change its contents.
Identify a tested artifact by its version or digest, then promote that same artifact between environments. Inject configuration from outside.
Recording the source commit and test results lets you track differences between the artifact that was tested and the one used in production.

example.scenario: Deploy to production after validation in staging.
steps: Build the artifact once.
Save the version and test results.
Promote the same artifact.
example.outcome: This avoids differences caused by rebuilding.

misconception.claim: Rebuilding for production is safer.
misconception.correction: Use the same artifact because rebuilding can create differences from the tested artifact.

takeaways: An artifact is a unit of distribution.
Promote the same artifact between environments.
Record the version, digest, and commit.

sections.title: Stop at gates and promote progressively
paragraphs: A quality gate is a checkpoint that verifies the conditions for moving to the next stage.
If monitoring metrics and functional checks meet the criteria in staging, proceed to the next stage. If they fail, stop the promotion and keep the healthy version running.
Document the success criteria, who is responsible when a failure occurs, the logs, and how to rerun. Do not lower thresholds for convenience.

example.scenario: Move an artifact from staging to production.
steps: Run tests and verify operation in staging.
Check whether the error rate is within the criteria.
If anything is wrong, do not promote; keep the healthy version running.
example.outcome: This limits the scope of a failure’s impact.

misconception.claim: Continue as scheduled even if a gate fails.
misconception.correction: If the conditions are not met, stop, resolve the cause, and then rerun.

takeaways: A gate is an explicit condition.
Progressive promotion limits impact.
When a failure occurs, preserve the healthy version and the evidence.

questions.title: Pipeline
questions.prompt: Choose the one incorrect statement about CI/CD.

choices.text: Source is the starting point for changes.
choices.explanation: The source stage brings in changes.

choices.text: Test detects issues early.
choices.explanation: Testing checks quality before deployment.

choices.text: Deploy always sends changes to production regardless of test results.
choices.explanation: The design must allow the pipeline to stop at a quality gate or for approval.

learning.reason: Review the workflow, including checks and points where it can stop.
learning.concept: A pipeline moves changes through a source and stages.

questions.title: Safe releases
questions.prompt: Select two statements that are incorrect about safe CI/CD operations.

choices.text: Run automated tests before production deployment.
choices.explanation: This is a gate that checks changes early.

choices.text: Continue deployment even if the build fails.
choices.explanation: A failed result stops the deployment.

choices.text: Do not keep a known-good version for rollback.
choices.explanation: Recovery capability must be ensured.

learning.reason: This question asks you to select the set of incorrect statements.
learning.concept: For a negatively worded question, record the items to be selected as correct.

questions.title: CI starting point
questions.prompt: Choose the one correct description of the role of a quality gate.

choices.text: Check the conditions for moving to the next stage, and stop progress if they are not met.
choices.explanation: A gate is a checkpoint that verifies success criteria. The process cannot move to the next stage until those criteria are met.

choices.text: If a check fails, skip it and move on to the next stage.
choices.explanation: Lowering the criteria to let the process pass goes against the role of a gate, which is to verify quality.

choices.text: When the scheduled time arrives, begin deployment regardless of the check results.
choices.explanation: A scheduled time cannot replace quality criteria. Stop progress if they are not met.

learning.reason: Make the criteria for moving to the next stage explicit, then proceed only after confirming they have been met.
learning.concept: A gate is a checkpoint that checks the conditions for moving forward.

questions.title: When CI Fails
questions.prompt: A required test failed, and a mismatch was recorded in the log. Choose one action that would be incorrect to take next.

choices.text: Check the failed required test’s log for the mismatch and fix the cause.
choices.explanation: The failure log helps narrow down the cause and identify what needs to be fixed.

choices.text: After the fix, rerun the required test with the same inputs and test conditions.
choices.explanation: Rerun the test under the same conditions to confirm that the required test passes after the fix.

choices.text: Proceed to deploy while leaving the log as is, even if a required test has failed.
choices.explanation: A required test failure must stop subsequent stages; fix the issue and rerun the test under the same conditions.

learning.reason: This tests whether you can decide to keep a failure from moving to later stages.
learning.concept: When CI fails, investigate and fix the cause.

questions.title: Benefits of CI
questions.prompt: Select two correct benefits of CI.

choices.text: It is easier to detect defects while changes are still small.
choices.explanation: Frequent integration helps narrow down the cause.

choices.text: If CI succeeds, there will definitely be no production incidents.
choices.explanation: CI does not guarantee everything.

choices.text: You can use build and test results to inform the next decision.
choices.explanation: Test results can be used for promotion.

choices.text: You can hide failures and still integrate.
choices.explanation: Failures are recorded and fixed.

choices.text: Approvals and monitoring become unnecessary.
choices.explanation: CI alone does not eliminate the need for operational decisions.

learning.reason: Connect the value and limitations of CI.
learning.concept: Explain the purpose of CI as it moves from commit to build and test.

questions.title: Delivery and deployment
questions.prompt: Choose one correct statement about delivery and deployment.

choices.text: Delivery always deploys to production without approval.
choices.explanation: Delivery means being ready for distribution.

choices.text: Deployment automates the process through production deployment after inspection.
choices.explanation: Continuous deployment proceeds all the way to production deployment.

choices.text: Deployment does not inspect artifacts.
choices.explanation: Gates are required even for automated deployment.

learning.reason: Review the difference between a deployable state and automated deployment.
learning.concept: Distinguish delivery, deployment, and approval.

questions.title: The Role of Approval
questions.prompt: Select the one incorrect step in a process that includes approval.

choices.text: Keep the inspected version as a candidate.
choices.explanation: You can identify the item before approval.

choices.text: Review the impact of the change and the monitoring plan.
choices.explanation: Approval is an operational checkpoint.

choices.text: Skip testing because the approver takes the place of test.
choices.explanation: Approval is not a substitute for automated checks.

learning.reason: To avoid confusing approval with automated checks.
learning.concept: Approval is a decision point separate from the quality gate.

questions.title: Delivery methods
questions.prompt: Select the 2 correct statements about delivery, deployment, and approvals.

choices.text: Delivery keeps software in a state that is ready for production.
choices.explanation: The core of delivery is maintaining a releasable state.

choices.text: Deployment always requires human approval.
choices.explanation: Continuous deployment can also happen without approval.

choices.text: Adding an approval means tests are no longer needed.
choices.explanation: Approval is not a substitute for testing.

choices.text: Approvals let you review the impact and monitoring plan.
choices.explanation: It is a checkpoint for assessing operational risk.

choices.text: Delivery rebuilds the artifact every time.
choices.explanation: Artifact identity is a separate design concern.

learning.reason: Assess delivery methods and approvals together.
learning.concept: Distinguish between delivery, deployment, and approval.

questions.title: Same artifact
questions.prompt: Choose the 2 incorrect statements about artifact promotion.

choices.text: Inspect an artifact built once, then promote that same artifact across environments.
choices.explanation: This reduces differences between the artifact tested and the one used in production.

choices.text: Build a separate artifact for each environment.
choices.explanation: Rebuilding can change the contents.

choices.text: Do not record the version or digest.
choices.explanation: Recording them is necessary to track identity.

learning.reason: Promoting a verified artifact is a fundamental practice.
learning.concept: Build an artifact once and promote that same artifact.

questions.title: Rebuild
questions.prompt: Choose the one correct procedure for promoting from staging to production.

choices.text: Check the digest verified in staging.
choices.explanation: This confirms that it is the same artifact.

choices.text: Distribute a separate artifact rebuilt for production.
choices.explanation: Avoid this because it creates a difference from the artifact that was verified.

choices.text: Because configuration can be injected externally, identifying the artifact to be distributed can be omitted.
choices.explanation: Separating configuration and verifying artifact identity are separate checks. Track by version or digest whether the executable being deployed is the same one that was verified.

learning.reason: This procedure keeps the verified target unchanged.
learning.concept: Promote the same artifact across environments.

questions.title: Artifact tracking
questions.prompt: Select the two correct ways to track artifacts securely.

choices.text: Store the version or digest.
choices.explanation: This identifies the item being distributed.

choices.text: Modify files for each environment.
choices.explanation: This breaks identity.

choices.text: Associate the source commit with the inspection results.
choices.explanation: This lets you trace provenance.

choices.text: Delete the inspected artifact and rebuild it.
choices.explanation: You cannot promote the same artifact.

choices.text: Treat artifacts as identical even when their digests differ.
choices.explanation: Different digests mean different artifacts.

learning.reason: This is a practical decision about recording identity and provenance.
learning.concept: Record the version, digest, commit, and inspection results.

questions.title: Staged promotion
questions.prompt: Select the 2 statements that are incorrect about staged promotion.

choices.text: Advance to production after checking the baseline in staging.
choices.explanation: Verify quality at each stage.

choices.text: Continue on schedule even if a gate fails.
choices.explanation: Stop if the conditions are not met.

choices.text: Decide who is responsible and how to rerun after a failure.
choices.explanation: Make the gate an effective stopping point.

choices.text: If failures continue, lower the threshold to pass.
choices.explanation: Resolve the cause without lowering the quality criteria.

choices.text: Ensure the previous healthy version can be maintained.
choices.explanation: Limit the impact of failures.

learning.reason: Assess stop conditions and failure responses together.
learning.concept: Stop failures with quality gates and staged promotion.

units.title: Testing and Quality Gates
units.summary: Learn test levels, reproducible expectations, quality gates, and failure investigation.
units.objective: Design checkpoints that prevent failures from reaching production.
explanation: Combine unit, integration, and E2E tests according to their purpose, and evaluate changes using fixed inputs and expected results.
Use quality gates to stop failures, and document their causes and how to prevent recurrence.
units.example: Verify calculations with unit tests and service-to-service connections with integration tests before running E2E tests.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what unit, integration, and E2E tests cover and when to use each.
Design reproducible tests using fixed inputs and expected results.
Apply inspection results progressively as quality gate conditions.
Investigate the failure and use the findings to create regression tests and address the root cause.

sections.title: Choosing the right test granularity
paragraphs: Unit tests verify small units such as functions and classes by checking how inputs correspond to results. They run quickly and make it easier to narrow down failures, but they do not verify connections to other services.

Integration tests check the boundaries between multiple modules or services. They find problems that arise from combining components, such as issues with actual data formats, authentication, communication, and persistence.

E2E tests exercise the entire system from an entry point close to the user’s actions. They can verify important business flows, but involve many environmental, data, and external dependencies, so they run slowly and failures can have many possible causes.
Start with small unit tests to check local rules, use integration tests for boundaries, and E2E tests for important user flows. Relying only on E2E tests slows down both fault isolation and feedback.

example.scenario: Calculate the order amount, connect to the inventory service, and display the order completion screen.
steps: Run a unit test on the tax calculation function with fixed inputs.
Run integration tests on the formats of the order API and inventory API.
Run an E2E test from the buyer’s login through to the completion screen.
example.outcome: Separating the failure scope handled by each test lets you combine fast checks with checks of important flows.

misconception.claim: If E2E tests pass, unit and integration tests are unnecessary.
misconception.correction: E2E tests check the overall flow, but unit tests that quickly pinpoint local causes and integration tests that check boundaries are also valuable.

takeaways: Unit tests check small rules, integration tests check boundaries, and E2E tests check user flows.
The larger the test scope, the greater the execution and failure investigation burden.
Choose tests based on their purpose and how failures will be investigated.

sections.title: Reproduce results with fixed inputs and expected values
paragraphs: A test is a check that sets up preconditions, provides input, and compares the result with what is expected. If the input changes every time, the same code can produce different results, making failures impossible to reproduce.

Control sources of variation such as time, randomness, external APIs, and shared data with fixed values, managed fixtures, or contract-defined responses. General-purpose unit mocks used for testing convenience are separate from the requirement to verify real boundaries in IT/E2E tests.

Determine expected values from the specification: not just whether the operation succeeded, but also return values, state changes, and error types. Specify expectations for boundary values and failures as well as the normal path.

Recording the reproduction steps, input, expected values, and actual results lets someone investigating a CI failure use the same conditions. For a calculation that derives a tax-inclusive amount from a tax-exclusive amount, where the tax rate changes based on the effective date and time, fix or record the effective date and time, tax rate, tax-exclusive amount, and expected tax-inclusive amount together.

example.scenario: Change a function that applies a discount rate.
steps: Fix the input amount at 1000, the discount rate at 10%, and the currency at JPY.
Set the expected value to 900 and determine rounding rules from the specification.
Make empty values and upper-limit values separate test cases too, and compare the results.
example.outcome: You can explain the effects of a change without being affected by the environment or execution time.

misconception.claim: Using random inputs for every test makes coverage comprehensive and reproducibility high.
misconception.correction: Even when using randomness, save the seed and failing input so you can rerun the test under the same conditions.

takeaways: Specify the inputs, preconditions, and expected values.
Control sources of variation and save failure conditions.
Distinguish unit mock usage from real-boundary verification in IT/E2E tests.

sections.title: Stop Failures at Quality Gates
paragraphs: A quality gate is a checkpoint that determines, automatically or through approval, whether conditions for proceeding to the next stage have been met. Set requirements such as a successful build, required type checks, passing unit/integration tests, passing critical E2E tests, and an acceptable failure rate according to the change risk.
Gate conditions make clear what is measured, the passing threshold, and what happens on failure. It is important not merely to run tests, but to prevent failed runs from proceeding to later stages.

Placing fast unit tests early and integration or E2E tests later lets you detect inexpensive failures first. However, include critical paths in the gate even if they take longer; do not sacrifice the purpose of the checks.
Save results as reports. CodeBuild test reports can be used to investigate test case successes and failures and trends, and can inform CI decisions.

example.scenario: Promote a new artifact from staging to production.
steps: Check whether all unit and integration tests have passed.
Check the criteria for critical E2E tests and the error rate.
If the criteria are not met, stop the promotion and save the report.
example.outcome: Treat test results as explicit conditions, and do not let failures reach production.

misconception.claim: A gate may pass as long as at least one test has run.
misconception.correction: Judge by whether the defined cases and passing criteria were met, not by whether tests ran at all.

takeaways: Specify the scope, passing criteria, and failure handling for each gate.
Place fast checks early and important end-to-end checks later.
Save failure reports and use them to inform the next decision.

sections.title: Investigate Failures and Prevent Regressions
paragraphs: Classify failed tests by possible causes, such as code defects, incorrect test data, or failures in the environment or dependent services. First, preserve the inputs, expected values, actual results, logs, and the commit containing the change, then reproduce the same failure.

Once you can reproduce it, reduce the case to the smallest failing example and identify the layer where the expected and actual results diverge. If the test itself is wrong, revisit the specification and expected values.
After fixing the cause, add a regression test that reproduces the failure so the gate can detect the same defect if it returns. Do not delete tests or lower thresholds just to make the fix pass.

For IT/E2E tests that use external services, verify the boundaries against the real services and design environment setup, cleanup, and data isolation. Do not confuse unit tests, which use mocks for testing convenience, with IT/E2E tests, which verify real integrations.

example.scenario: An order E2E test failed in CI, and the screen displayed an inventory error.
steps: Save the commit from the failure, the input order, the logs, and the expected screen.
Rerun unit, integration, and E2E tests in that order to identify the first mismatch.
Fix the cause and add the same inventory shortage condition as a regression test.
example.outcome: You can verify the cause and prevent recurrence instead of stopping after a temporary rerun.

misconception.claim: If a test fails only once, just delete it so CI passes.
misconception.correction: Investigate the reproduction conditions, fix the environment if needed, and keep a regression test that addresses the cause.

takeaways: Reproduce failures using the inputs, expected values, actual results, and logs.
Isolate the cause layer by layer.
After a fix, use a regression test to capture recurrence at the gate.

questions.title: Test granularity
questions.prompt: Choose the one correct description of unit, integration, and E2E tests.

choices.text: Unit tests check small units, integration tests check boundaries, and E2E tests check user journeys.
choices.explanation: Their scopes differ.

choices.text: E2E tests are always faster than unit tests and make it easier to identify the cause.
choices.explanation: E2E tests depend on many environmental factors, so they tend to be slower and the possible cause is harder to narrow down.

choices.text: Integration tests check only the return value of a single function.
choices.explanation: A single function is the concern of a unit test; integration tests check boundaries.

learning.reason: Learn to distinguish test scopes, from small units to user journeys.
learning.concept: Distinguish the roles of unit, integration, and E2E tests.

questions.title: Choosing test granularity
questions.prompt: Choose the one incorrect statement about where to place tests.

choices.text: Check tax calculation rules with unit tests.
choices.explanation: Local calculation rules can be checked quickly with unit tests.

choices.text: Check data formats between APIs with integration tests.
choices.explanation: Combinations across service boundaries are the focus of integration tests.

choices.text: Rely only on end-to-end tests of the full interface to sufficiently identify the cause of failures in individual functions.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. End-to-end tests cover a broad range of possible causes, so support from unit tests and other tests is needed.

learning.reason: Place tests based on their scope and how easy it is to investigate failures.
learning.concept: Combine test granularities instead of relying only on large-scale tests.

questions.title: Test combinations
questions.prompt: Choose 2 correct approaches to designing tests for order processing.

choices.text: Verify calculation logic with unit tests and service integrations with integration tests.
choices.explanation: Test local rules and boundaries at the appropriate levels of granularity.

choices.text: Add more E2E tests only, with no unit or integration tests.
choices.explanation: This makes it take longer to identify causes and leaves boundaries insufficiently tested.

choices.text: In integration tests, always perform only screen interactions.
choices.explanation: Testing the entire UI is closer to E2E; integration tests focus on boundaries.

choices.text: Use E2E tests to verify the critical path from login through order completion.
choices.explanation: This tests an end-to-end flow that is close to the user's experience.

choices.text: Use the same number of tests for every type without defining their purpose.
choices.explanation: Choose test granularity according to purpose and risk.

learning.reason: This is the judgment involved in breaking a feature down into three layers for testing.
learning.concept: Combine unit, integration, and E2E tests according to their purpose.

questions.title: Expected Values
questions.prompt: Choose 2 statements that describe reproducible tests.

choices.text: Compare fixed inputs with expected values defined by the specification.
choices.explanation: Conditions and criteria are explicit, making it easier to reproduce the same result.

choices.text: Change the execution time each time and determine the expected value after execution.
choices.explanation: If you determine the expected value afterward, it is not a test.

choices.text: Record the inputs and actual results when a test fails.
choices.explanation: With this evidence, you can rerun the test under the same conditions and investigate.

learning.reason: Fixing the inputs and expected values in advance lets you objectively compare the results of a change.
learning.concept: A test makes its assumptions, inputs, expected values, and actual results explicit.

questions.title: Variable Factors
questions.prompt: Select 2 statements that are incorrect about test design.

choices.text: When using random numbers, save the seed and the inputs that caused failures.
choices.explanation: This makes it possible to rerun the test under the same conditions.

choices.text: Even if responses from an external API change each time, there is no need to record the inputs and expected values.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Control sources of variability and record the conditions and results.

choices.text: Do not define expected values for boundary cases or failures.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Define expected values for boundary and error cases based on the specifications.

learning.reason: Make tests reproducible by controlling variable external factors rather than leaving them unchecked.
learning.concept: Design reproducible tests using fixed inputs and expected values.

questions.title: Boundary validation
questions.prompt: Choose two correct approaches to designing inputs and expected values.

choices.text: Make the values concrete, such as an amount of 1000, a 10% discount, and an expected value of 900.
choices.explanation: You can compare the fixed conditions with the expected result.

choices.text: Adjust the expected value to match the actual result so the test passes.
choices.explanation: Set the expected value from the specification; do not change it to match the result.

choices.text: Create separate cases for boundary conditions such as maximum values and empty values.
choices.explanation: This can detect specification violations at boundaries.

choices.text: Do not control time or random values, and do not retain the seed when a failure occurs.
choices.explanation: You cannot reproduce the same failure.

choices.text: Replace all IT/E2E tests that check external boundaries with unit mocks alone.
choices.explanation: This defeats the purpose of checking actual integration.

learning.reason: Combine fixed conditions, boundary values, and external boundaries in one test design.
learning.concept: Control inputs, expected values, and sources of variation to keep tests reproducible.

questions.title: Quality gate
questions.prompt: Choose one correct statement about quality gates.

choices.text: Do not allow a change to proceed to the next stage unless it meets the defined checks and acceptance criteria.
choices.explanation: A gate is a condition that stops promotion.

choices.text: Always pass a change solely because the tests were run.
choices.explanation: The results must meet the criteria; merely running the tests is not enough.

choices.text: Deleting a failed check satisfies the quality gate.
choices.explanation: Hiding a failure is not quality assurance.

learning.reason: A gate is judged by the results and acceptance criteria, not by whether the checks were run.
learning.concept: A quality gate is a stopping point that prevents failures from reaching production.

questions.title: Staged gates
questions.prompt: Choose the one statement that is incorrect about staged quality gates.

choices.text: Run fast unit tests early to detect failures quickly.
choices.explanation: Placing inexpensive checks first speeds up feedback.

choices.text: Include critical E2E tests as a later-stage promotion condition.
choices.explanation: Proceed only after checking the critical paths end to end.

choices.text: Because E2E tests are slow, ignore failures on critical paths and deploy.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Include necessary checks in the gate, even when they are slow.

learning.reason: This means distinguishing speed from the importance of checks and not skipping necessary checks.
learning.concept: Staging tests does not mean lowering quality criteria.

questions.title: Gate conditions
questions.prompt: Select the 2 statements that are incorrect as a quality gate design.

choices.text: Clearly document the tests in scope, pass criteria, and how failures will be handled.
choices.explanation: This makes the conditions for reproducing the decision clear.

choices.text: When the failure rate is high, lower the threshold to make the gate pass.
choices.explanation: Investigate the cause without lowering the criteria.

choices.text: Approve based on the memory of someone who viewed the screen, without saving a report.
choices.explanation: Without evidence, you cannot investigate trends or causes later.

choices.text: Investigate successes, failures, and trends in CodeBuild test reports.
choices.explanation: You can use test results for the next quality decision.

choices.text: Save test results as a report and use it as evidence for the gate.
choices.explanation: Saving test results is a sound practice that supports quality decisions and failure investigations.

learning.reason: Combining decision criteria with evidence makes the gate operational.
learning.concept: Design quality gates around scope, criteria, results, and failure handling.

questions.title: Failure investigation
questions.prompt: Choose one correct response to a CI test failure.

choices.text: Reproduce the failure with the inputs, expected values, actual results, logs, and commit fixed.
choices.explanation: Reproducing the same conditions makes it possible to investigate the cause.

choices.text: If it fails once, discard the logs and simply rerun the test.
choices.explanation: This loses evidence of the cause and of measures to prevent recurrence.

choices.text: Delete the test without checking the cause.
choices.explanation: The defect can no longer be detected.

learning.reason: Begin investigating only after turning the failure into evidence that can be used to reproduce it.
learning.concept: Failure investigation fixes the inputs, expected values, results, logs, and changes in place.

questions.title: Regression Prevention
questions.prompt: Choose the one option that is incorrect as a way to prevent regressions after a failure.

choices.text: Create a minimal case that reproduces the failure.
choices.explanation: This helps narrow down the layer and conditions causing the issue.

choices.text: After fixing the cause, add a regression test under the same conditions.
choices.explanation: A gate can detect recurrence of the same defect.

choices.text: If the fix passes, do not add a test to prevent recurrence.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Keep the regression test to detect future recurrence.

learning.reason: This is the decision to carry the failure conditions forward into future checks, rather than stopping at the fix.
learning.concept: Prevent the same defect with a fix for its cause and a regression test.

questions.title: Learning from Failures
questions.prompt: Select the two statements that are incorrect about failure investigation and IT/E2E practices.

choices.text: Isolate the first discrepancy by layer, then add a regression test that addresses its cause.
choices.explanation: This identifies the cause and enables automatic detection of recurrence.

choices.text: Always replace IT/E2E tests with unit mocks alone, without checking real boundaries.
choices.explanation: Integration problems will no longer be detectable.

choices.text: Rerun the test without isolating shared data that another test may change.
choices.explanation: When changes from another test get mixed in, it is impossible to isolate the cause of the failure and the conditions needed to reproduce it.

choices.text: Design environment setup, data isolation, and cleanup for IT/E2E tests.
choices.explanation: This verifies real boundaries while keeping the environment reproducible.

choices.text: Record the cause of the failure and any unresolved points, and use them in the next investigation.
choices.explanation: Recording the results and unresolved points supports the next hypothesis test and helps prevent recurrence.

learning.reason: Treat cause isolation, verification of real boundaries, and data isolation as a connected improvement process.
learning.concept: Connect failure investigation to regression prevention and reproducible IT/E2E practices.

units.title: Deployment and Recovery
units.summary: Decide on progressive delivery, monitoring, stopping, rollback, and data compatibility.
units.objective: Choose progressive delivery, approval, and rollback.
explanation: Gradually shift between the old and new versions, and stop or recover if the observed metrics fall outside the criteria.
Design code rollback and data recovery separately, and check compatibility.
units.example: Send a small amount of traffic to the new version with a canary, and revert to the old version if the error rate exceeds the threshold.

learningObjectives.text: Compare the deployment scope and risks of rolling, blue/green, and canary deployments.
Continue or stop the phased rollout based on observed values and stop criteria.
Choose rollback or rollforward according to the situation, and explain the recovery procedure.
Design safe recovery that accounts for DB change compatibility and backup/restore.

sections.title: Control blast radius with deployment strategies
paragraphs: A rolling deployment replaces running instances with the new version a few at a time. You can update without taking the whole system offline, but you need to account for the period when old and new versions run at the same time and for the capacity that remains available.

A blue/green deployment runs the old blue environment alongside the new green environment for validation, then switches traffic. You can check green before the switch and more easily return to blue if there is a problem, but this requires double the resources.

A canary deployment initially sends only a small amount of traffic to the new version, then expands the scope after observation. You can validate with real traffic, but you need to decide how to select targets, set stages and wait times, and define stop conditions.

Choose a strategy based on acceptable downtime, additional cost, the blast radius of the change, and rollback speed. Do not assume a strategy is safe based on its name alone; also check the conditions for running the old and new versions side by side.

example.scenario: Deploy a new version of a payment API to production.
steps: Compare the constraints of rolling, blue/green, and canary deployments to avoid downtime.
First, send a small amount of real traffic to the new version with a canary deployment.
Increase traffic in stages once the criteria are met.
example.outcome: You can detect production issues while keeping the blast radius small.

misconception.claim: With blue/green, you can always roll back safely without considering data or traffic switching.
misconception.correction: Even with two environments, you need to design traffic switching, shared data, compatibility, and monitoring separately.

takeaways: Rolling replaces instances a few at a time, blue/green switches environments, and canary starts with a small amount of traffic.
Check the conditions for running old and new versions side by side and the resource costs.
Choose a strategy based on the blast radius and recovery method.

sections.title: Observe and Apply Abort Criteria
paragraphs: During deployment, compare metrics such as error rate, latency, traffic, and saturation between the old and new versions. Also check whether errors are increasing in users’ critical operations.

Define abort criteria numerically in advance—for example, when the error rate exceeds the acceptable value, p95 latency exceeds the established value, or a health check fails. For instance, if the abort threshold for the error rate is set at 2% and 3% is observed during a canary, the threshold has been exceeded. A vague instruction such as “stop if there’s a problem” delays decision-making.

For canary or blue/green deployments, decide how long to wait for observations and how to roll traffic back. If a threshold is exceeded, do not proceed to the next stage; save the evidence and investigate the cause.

Even when monitoring looks healthy, unmeasured business errors can go unnoticed. Combine technical metrics with important business outcomes, and do not expand the deployment when the state cannot be observed.

example.scenario: The new version’s p95 latency exceeded the baseline during a canary.
steps: Compare latency, error rate, and business success rate between the old and new versions.
Check the abort threshold defined in advance.
Stop expanding traffic, roll back to the old version, and save the logs and deployment ID.
example.outcome: You can stop based on observed values rather than intuition and investigate the cause later.

misconception.claim: If CPU is normal, there is no user impact, so it is fine to continue the deployment.
misconception.correction: Check metrics that reflect the change’s impact, such as errors, latency, and business success rate, not just CPU.

takeaways: Define observation metrics and abort thresholds in advance.
When a threshold is exceeded, stop expanding and roll traffic back if necessary.
Combine technical and business metrics.

sections.title: Choosing rollback or rollforward
paragraphs: Rollback means returning to a known-good version. In CodeDeploy, rollback redistributes a previous revision as a new deployment, so it does not simply rewind time.
Rollforward means moving ahead with a new revision that fixes the problem. Choose it when the cause lies in the configuration or code and you can safely validate the fix in a short time.

First, limit the impact by taking steps such as routing traffic back to the previous version, stopping the deployment, or turning off a feature flag. Then investigate the cause and determine the recovery scope.

Rollback does not always succeed. Rehearse compatibility between the old and new versions, external dependencies, changed data, and the permissions required for the procedure. Set the recovery time and identify who is responsible for the decision.

example.scenario: The order success rate dropped in the new version.
steps: Check the abort criteria and route canary traffic back to the previous version.
Isolate changes to the code, configuration, dependencies, and data.
Approve whether to roll forward with a fix or roll back to a known-good revision.
example.outcome: You can first stop the impact, then choose a recovery method without confusing it with the cause.

misconception.claim: Rolling back the code automatically returns changed data to its previous state.
misconception.correction: Code and data are separate states. Prepare separate data recovery procedures, such as backups, reverse transformations, or compatibility design.

takeaways: Rollback returns to a known-good version; rollforward advances with a fix.
First, stop traffic or functionality to limit the impact.
Rehearse recovery success, including coexistence of old and new versions and the state of the data.

sections.title: Designing Database Compatibility and Recovery
paragraphs: When new and old application versions run at the same time during a deployment, you need to preserve data formats and APIs that both versions can read. Add columns in a way that old versions can ignore, and schedule deletions or changes in meaning for a time when the old versions are no longer running.
A safe change follows a staged process: first add compatible columns or tables, then switch the code to the new format, and remove the old format only after no code uses it.
Creating a backup alone does not complete recovery. Actually verify the restoration procedure, restore destination, RPO/RTO, integrity checks, and application reconnection.

Rolling back only the code after data destruction or an irreversible conversion will not restore past data. Include reversible migrations, retained snapshots, and handling of changes made after recovery in the change plan.

example.scenario: Add a new shipping category to orders and perform a rolling deployment.
steps: First add a nullable column that old versions can ignore.
Deploy the code with a period during which both old and new versions can read the data.
After the old version is no longer needed, remove constraints or old columns in a separate change.
example.outcome: This avoids format mismatches while old and new versions run together, and lets you recover the code and DB together.

misconception.claim: Because there is a snapshot, rolling back only the code restores the original state even after a destructive migration.
misconception.correction: Restoration from the snapshot and checks for data loss and differences are required. Changing only the code version does not restore the DB state.

takeaways: Design schemas and APIs that allow old and new versions to coexist.
Separate addition, switching, and removal, and defer destructive changes to a later stage.
Perform backup restore exercises and integrity checks.

questions.title: Deployment strategies
questions.prompt: Choose the one correct description of rolling, blue/green, and canary deployments.

choices.text: A canary deployment sends a small amount of traffic to the new version, then expands the scope after observation.
choices.explanation: A canary deployment gradually exposes the new version to users.

choices.text: A blue/green deployment deletes the old environment before creating the new one.
choices.explanation: This approach runs the old and new environments side by side, validates them, and switches traffic.

choices.text: A rolling deployment switches all traffic to the new environment at once.
choices.explanation: A rolling deployment replaces instances or tasks a few at a time.

learning.reason: Distinguish how the three strategies handle traffic and environments.
learning.concept: Explain the characteristics of rolling, blue/green, and canary deployments.

questions.title: Choosing a Strategy
questions.prompt: Select the one incorrect statement about deployment strategies.

choices.text: Consider blue/green when you can accommodate duplicate resources and want to validate before switching over.
choices.explanation: You can validate the old and new environments side by side.

choices.text: Consider canary when you want to assess the impact using a small amount of real traffic.
choices.explanation: You can check in the live environment while limiting the blast radius.

choices.text: With rolling deployments, there is no period when the old and new versions run at the same time.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Because instances are replaced gradually, there is a period when the old and new versions coexist.

learning.reason: Determine whether versions coexist during deployment and whether additional resources are needed.
learning.concept: Compare the risks and constraints of each strategy.

questions.title: Comparing deployment strategies
questions.prompt: Select the two correct judgments when choosing a strategy.

choices.text: If you want to avoid downtime and can afford the cost of running two environments, compare blue/green deployment.
choices.explanation: This takes into account the trade-off of validating before the switch and keeping the old environment running.

choices.text: Deploy based on the strategy name alone, without deciding on DB compatibility or traffic switching.
choices.explanation: Coexistence conditions and data state also need to be designed.

choices.text: Canary deployment exposes the change to a small number of users, so monitoring is unnecessary.
choices.explanation: Monitor the impact on real traffic, even when only a small number of users are exposed.

choices.text: For canary deployment, which starts with a limited impact, define the stages, waiting periods, and stop conditions.
choices.explanation: This makes decisions about expanding the rollout reproducible.

choices.text: With rolling deployment, you don't need to consider the remaining capacity.
choices.explanation: Check capacity and availability during replacement.

learning.reason: Compare strategies by considering coexistence requirements and stop conditions, as well as their benefits.
learning.concept: Choose a strategy based on downtime tolerance, cost, scope of impact, and recovery speed.

questions.title: Abort criteria
questions.prompt: Select 2 correct decisions for aborting during a deployment.

choices.text: Stop the rollout if the predefined error rate or latency threshold is exceeded.
choices.explanation: Stop based on quantified criteria.

choices.text: If CPU is normal, do not check the error rate.
choices.explanation: Monitor user impact beyond CPU as well.

choices.text: If monitoring is unavailable, stop expanding traffic, save the logs, and investigate the cause.
choices.explanation: Do not treat an unobservable state as normal; stop the expansion and preserve evidence.

learning.reason: Stop by linking observed values to predefined criteria.
learning.concept: State abort criteria explicitly using metrics and thresholds.

questions.title: Observation
questions.prompt: Select two incorrect responses to a canary deployment.

choices.text: Compare the error rate, latency, and business success rate of the old and new versions.
choices.explanation: Check the impact of the change using multiple metrics.

choices.text: Expand traffic, assuming there is no problem even if some monitoring data is missing.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. If the system cannot be observed, do not expand traffic; establish the measurements first.

choices.text: Continue even after a threshold is exceeded, without saving the deployment ID and logs.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Stop, preserve the evidence, and proceed with an investigation into the cause.

learning.reason: Do not treat an unobservable state as normal; apply the stop conditions.
learning.concept: Monitor technical and business metrics, and do not expand when data is missing.

questions.title: Abort Criteria Combinations
questions.prompt: Select the two statements that are incorrect about monitoring and abort criteria.

choices.text: Decide in advance on the thresholds, waiting period, and action to restore traffic.
choices.explanation: This makes decisions and actions reproducible.

choices.text: Continue if CPU is normal, even when the business success rate deteriorates.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Deterioration in business metrics is also a reason to stop.

choices.text: When a threshold is exceeded, do not proceed to the next stage; save the logs.
choices.explanation: This limits the impact and preserves evidence.

choices.text: Compare metrics for the old and new versions under the same conditions.
choices.explanation: You can assess the impact of the change from the differences.

choices.text: Treat metrics that are not being measured as normal and expand the rollout.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. You cannot make a safe decision when observability is unavailable.

learning.reason: Review stop decisions based on metric types and whether they can be observed.
learning.concept: Control a staged rollout using monitoring and abort criteria.

questions.title: rollback
questions.prompt: Choose the one correct statement about rollback and rollforward.

choices.text: rollback returns to a known good version, while rollforward advances a fix as a new revision.
choices.explanation: The two differ in the direction and target of recovery.

choices.text: rollback also automatically restores the database to an earlier state.
choices.explanation: Code recovery and data recovery must be designed separately.

choices.text: CodeDeploy rollback only restores a past deployment in time.
choices.explanation: It redistributes a previous revision as a new deployment.

learning.reason: Separate recovery of application revisions from data recovery.
learning.concept: rollback and rollforward are different recovery strategies.

questions.title: Recovery procedure
questions.prompt: Choose one statement that is incorrect about recovery procedures during an incident.

choices.text: First, reduce the impact by directing traffic back to the previous version or stopping the deployment.
choices.explanation: This limits the impact while the cause is being investigated.

choices.text: Check the cause and choose whether to proceed with a fix or return to a healthy revision.
choices.explanation: Choose rollforward or rollback based on the situation.

choices.text: Consider the task complete as soon as you perform a rollback once, without confirming that recovery succeeded.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Check health, business outcomes, and data consistency.

learning.reason: Recovery includes not only performing the recovery operation but also verifying the system afterward.
learning.concept: Treat impact containment, cause investigation, recovery, and verification as one continuous procedure.

questions.title: Recovery Strategy
questions.prompt: Select two correct decisions about rollback and rollforward.

choices.text: Return traffic to a known-good revision to stop the impact quickly.
choices.explanation: This is the basic operation for limiting impact with a rollback.

choices.text: Reverting the code always restores destroyed data too.
choices.explanation: Data requires a separate recovery procedure.

choices.text: Even when the cause is unknown, remove the threshold and send all traffic again.
choices.explanation: Do not expand the impact without confirming the cause and the criteria.

choices.text: Choose rollforward when the cause is known and the fix can be safely validated.
choices.explanation: This is the decision to advance the fix as a new revision.

choices.text: There is no need to check the business success rate after recovery.
choices.explanation: Verify both the technical state and the business outcome.

learning.reason: Assess impact containment, the cause, the fix, and recovery verification together.
learning.concept: Design the choice between rollback and rollforward, along with recovery verification.

questions.title: Database compatibility
questions.prompt: Choose the one correct approach to a deployment that involves a database change.

choices.text: Separate the addition, code switch, and removal of the old format, allowing a period when the old and new versions can coexist.
choices.explanation: This allows the old version running during a rolling deployment to handle the new schema.

choices.text: Delete the column used by the old version immediately after adding a new column.
choices.explanation: This is a breaking change that prevents the old version from working.

choices.text: There is no need to rehearse restoration because a backup exists.
choices.explanation: Restore capability and data consistency must be verified in practice.

learning.reason: Plan for old and new code to coexist, and defer breaking changes until a later stage.
learning.concept: Make database migrations gradual changes that preserve compatibility.

questions.title: Data Recovery
questions.prompt: Choose one incorrect statement about database recovery.

choices.text: After restoring from a snapshot, verify data consistency and that the application can reconnect.
choices.explanation: Check availability after the restore operation, too.

choices.text: Even after a destructive migration, rolling back the code alone restores the data to its previous state.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The code and database state are separate; restoring from a backup, for example, is necessary.

choices.text: Include recovery time and acceptable data loss in the plan.
choices.explanation: Reflect RTO/RPO in the recovery design.

learning.reason: Assess recoverability by distinguishing the code version from the data state.
learning.concept: Recovery after data destruction requires backup/restore and consistency validation.

questions.title: Safe Database Deployments
questions.prompt: Select two statements that are incorrect about database compatibility and recovery.

choices.text: Add the schema first in a way that the old version can ignore.
choices.explanation: This is a gradual change that allows the old and new versions to coexist.

choices.text: Immediately change to a column that the old version cannot read, even while a rolling deployment is in progress.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. It breaks compatibility with the old version.

choices.text: After restoring a backup, check consistency, differences, and reconnection.
choices.explanation: This verifies availability after restoration.

choices.text: Perform an irreversible transformation only after preparing a snapshot and recovery procedure.
choices.explanation: This ensures in advance that there is a way to restore the data state.

choices.text: Assume that a code rollback alone will also restore deleted database data.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Data requires a separate restore or compensating process.

learning.reason: Assess coexistence of old and new versions, irreversible changes, and restore verification as one recovery plan.
learning.concept: Design database compatibility and backup/restore separately from code deployment.

units.title: Monitoring and Improvement
units.summary: Use metrics, logs, and traces to understand system conditions, then verify improvements against goals and hypotheses.
units.objective: Measure the impact on users, validate hypotheses through observation, and confirm improvements.
explanation: Observability is not about collecting numbers; it is about explaining system conditions and choosing what to investigate next.
units.example: Even when the HTTP failure rate and CPU utilization rise at the same time, verify the hypothesis with traces and logs before taking action.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish which questions metrics, logs, and traces can answer.
Interpret latency, errors, traffic, and saturation in terms of user impact and resource state.
Define the denominator, observation window, threshold, and handling of missing data for SLIs, SLOs, and alerts.
Form hypotheses from observations, test them without mistaking correlation for causation, and confirm whether they lead to improvement.

sections.title: Three Signals: Numbers, Events, and Request Paths
paragraphs: A metric is a numerical value collected at regular intervals. It is useful for questions that compare changes or trends on a graph, such as request counts, p95 latency, and CPU utilization. In CloudWatch, system performance data published by AWS services or users is treated as metrics.

A log records an event that occurred at a particular point in time. It helps investigate in detail what happened with a specific request, using information such as an error code, request ID, or exception message. Design logs to form a consistent, searchable timeline and to avoid exposing secret values.

A trace connects the sequence in which a single request passes through the frontend, services, databases, and other components. It lets you see which downstream call consumed time for a slow request. Use all three together: detect anomalies with metrics, then narrow down the target with logs and traces.

example.scenario: The order API’s p95 latency increased.
steps: Use metrics to check when and for which operation latency started increasing.
Use logs from the same time period to narrow down errors and the relevant request ID.
Use traces to see which downstream call consumed time for the slow request.
example.outcome: Because numbers, events, and request paths each serve a different role, do not determine the cause from graphs alone.

misconception.claim: If logs are available, metrics and traces are unnecessary.
misconception.correction: Logs are useful for individual events, while metrics add trends and traces add paths between services.

takeaways: Metrics show numerical trends.
Logs show time-stamped events.
Traces show the path of a single request.

sections.title: Four ways to look: Separate user impact from remaining capacity
paragraphs: Latency is the time a response takes; errors are failed requests; traffic is the volume of requests; and saturation describes how much processing capacity is being used. Looking at all four at once helps distinguish whether users are experiencing delays, requests are failing, load has increased, or resources have little capacity left.

Averages can hide slow experiences for some users. For example, p95 latency is a metric for examining experiences on the slower side compared with most requests. Before interpreting the value, however, clarify the operation being measured, the aggregation period, and the unit.

A simultaneous rise in CPU and HTTP 5xx is a clue for investigation. But we cannot yet say that high CPU caused the 5xx errors. An increase in the length of a processing queue or in the number of waiting requests can indicate saturation, where processing capacity has little room to spare. Add observations of traffic changes, dependency failures, traces, and logs, then compare hypotheses that could explain what you see.

example.scenario: HTTP 5xx and CPU utilization rise only at midday.
steps: Check whether traffic increases during the same time period.
Check user impact by looking at latency and errors for each operation.
Use traces and logs to compare possible causes such as dependency failures, timeouts, and resource exhaustion.
example.outcome: Treat the two values that rose together as correlated, then use additional observations to narrow down possible causes.

misconception.claim: If 5xx errors increased when CPU was high, that proves CPU is the cause.
misconception.correction: Changes that occur together show correlation. Do not conclude that one caused the other until observations verify other factors, such as traffic or dependencies.

takeaways: Latency and errors show user impact.
Traffic and saturation show load and remaining capacity.
Correlation is the starting point for a hypothesis.

sections.title: SLI, SLO, alert: what to report, by when, and under what conditions
paragraphs: An SLI is a measurement that represents service health. For example, “the number of requests to the Orders API that succeeded within 500ms over the past 28 days ÷ the total number of in-scope requests” makes the numerator and denominator explicit: good events and all in-scope events. A success rate without a defined denominator cannot distinguish periods with no requests from missed measurements.

An SLO is a target for an SLI. Set the threshold, target, and observation window, for example, “at least 99.9% over 28 days.” Choose the observation window in advance, including whether it is calendar-based or rolling, so short-lived incidents and long-term quality are not treated the same way.

An alert reports a condition that requires a person to act. Define the scope, success criteria, denominator, and observation window in the SLO; specify recipients, the threshold that triggers a notification, and how to handle missing data separately as operational settings. Automatically treating missing data as healthy can cause measurement outages to go unnoticed. Use a separate heartbeat or traffic signal to determine whether “no data” means “there were no requests” or “the measurement system stopped,” and set a threshold the recipients can act on.

example.scenario: Create an availability SLO for the Orders API.
steps: Define the in-scope operation, success criteria, numerator, and denominator.
Choose a 28-day rolling window and a target and threshold of 99.9%.
Decide how to distinguish zero requests from missing measurements, and define the steps to take after a notification.
example.outcome: The result is an SLO and alert that explain not just the numbers, but also what is included in the calculation and when observations are missing.

misconception.claim: A period with no data points is always healthy.
misconception.correction: No requests is different from a failed measurement. Use another observation to determine what missing data means.

takeaways: An SLI is a measurement with a numerator and denominator.
An SLO is a target with a threshold and an observation window.
An alert defines what missing data means and what action to take.

sections.title: Improvement: Test hypotheses and compare results
paragraphs: Troubleshooting is an iterative process: use observations and how the system works to form hypotheses about possible causes, then look for evidence that supports or refutes them. First, establish the time, affected operation, user impact, and recent changes so you have a basis for comparison.

If you make a fix based on a single correlation, you may mistake coincidental changes for the cause. Even when HTTP 5xx errors and high CPU occur together, compare increased traffic, downstream database latency, and deployments using traces, logs, and metrics, then choose a test that limits impact.

After an improvement, don’t stop at “CPU went down.” Compare the same SLI, observation window, and affected operation before and after the change. Check whether user impact, such as errors or latency, improved and whether anything worsened. Record the results and unresolved questions for the next hypothesis.

example.scenario: I want to improve the order API by changing the connection pool settings.
steps: Observe 5xx errors, p95 latency, traffic, CPU, and traces, then form a hypothesis that connections are waiting on a downstream service.
Change the settings in a limited-impact environment or through a gradual rollout.
Compare the SLI and traces before and after the change over the same observation window, and check whether the improvement supports the hypothesis.
example.outcome: You can evaluate the change by looking at improved user impact without concluding that the correlation between CPU and 5xx errors proves the cause.

misconception.claim: If CPU goes down after a change, that proves users are better off.
misconception.correction: CPU is a resource metric. Compare user impact, such as errors or latency for the affected operation, under the same conditions.

takeaways: Use observations to support or refute hypotheses.
Correlation does not prove causation.
Compare improvements using the same SLI and observation window.

questions.title: metric
questions.prompt: Choose the best description of a metric.

choices.text: A value compared over time, such as the number of requests or p95 latency.
choices.explanation: A metric is a value that represents system performance or trends.

choices.text: Only the order of services traversed by a single request.
choices.explanation: This is the path primarily covered by a trace.

choices.text: Only individual events that include an exception message or request ID.
choices.explanation: These are details primarily covered by a log.

learning.reason: Separate the questions asked about each signal.
learning.concept: A metric is a value used to read trends.

questions.title: Slow Request
questions.prompt: After p95 latency increases, choose one thing that can show which downstream call a slow request spent time on.

choices.text: CPU average only.
choices.explanation: It shows resource status, but not the request path.

choices.text: A trace linking that request.
choices.explanation: A trace can track the path and timing of a single request, including downstream services.

choices.text: SLO target value only.
choices.explanation: An SLO is a quality target, not details of an individual request path.

learning.reason: Move the investigation from the metric to the path.
learning.concept: A trace is the route a request takes.

questions.title: Choosing the Right Signal
questions.prompt: Choose the one correct way to use metrics, logs, and traces.

choices.text: Rely on logs alone to assess long-term trends and request paths in the same way.
choices.explanation: Logs are good for detail, while metrics and traces help with trends and paths.

choices.text: Use traces alone to determine error messages and total request volume.
choices.explanation: Traces show request paths; other signals provide detailed events and aggregated values.

choices.text: Use metrics to spot when an anomaly occurred, then use logs and traces to narrow down the target and path.
choices.explanation: This approach combines the complementary roles of all three signals.

learning.reason: Don’t place too much trust in any one signal.
learning.concept: Combine numbers, events, and paths.

questions.title: Four Signals
questions.prompt: Choose the one incorrect statement about latency, errors, traffic, and saturation.

choices.text: Latency measures response time.
choices.explanation: It indicates how long users wait.

choices.text: Errors measure failed requests.
choices.explanation: Check the failure rate or number of failures.

choices.text: Traffic measures request volume.
choices.explanation: It is used to check changes in load.

choices.text: Saturation is always the HTTP success rate itself.
choices.explanation: That is incorrect. Saturation indicates the remaining capacity of resources or processing capability.

learning.reason: Separate user impact from remaining capacity.
learning.concept: The four signals represent different conditions.

questions.title: CPU and 5xx
questions.prompt: CPU utilization and HTTP 5xx errors rose at the same time during the day. Choose the one statement that is incorrect as an initial judgment.

choices.text: Conclude that high CPU is the cause of the 5xx errors and that no further observations are needed.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Simultaneous changes indicate correlation; check additional signals such as traffic and dependencies.

choices.text: Check traffic and operation-level latency over the same period.
choices.explanation: Observe load and user impact separately.

choices.text: Compare dependency failures and timeouts using traces and logs.
choices.explanation: Compare possible causes using additional evidence.

learning.reason: Do not assume correlation proves causation.
learning.concept: Compare hypotheses using additional observations.

questions.title: How to Read p95
questions.prompt: When investigating changes in response time, select 2 correct answers.

choices.text: You can always understand the impact on slow users from the average alone.
choices.explanation: The average can hide some slow requests.

choices.text: Look at p95 after clarifying the operation being measured and the aggregation period.
choices.explanation: Fix what you compare and over which window.

choices.text: If CPU is high, there is no need to measure latency.
choices.explanation: Check resource conditions and user impact separately.

choices.text: Do not look at errors and traffic because they are unrelated to latency.
choices.explanation: Looking at them together helps distinguish the situation.

choices.text: Consider increased traffic and saturation as possible causes as well.
choices.explanation: You can compare load with available capacity.

learning.reason: Do not draw conclusions from a single number.
learning.concept: Read user impact together with available capacity.
