questions.title: SLI
questions.prompt: Choose the two correct descriptions of defining the success rate of the order API as an SLI.

choices.text: Define the number of successful eligible requests as the numerator.
choices.explanation: This clarifies the favorable event.

choices.text: Define the number of eligible requests as the denominator.
choices.explanation: This clarifies the scope.

choices.text: Represent quality using only the number of successful requests, without defining a denominator.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Without the total number of eligible requests, you cannot determine the success rate or whether there is no data.

learning.reason: This makes the measurement target explainable.
learning.concept: An SLI has a numerator and a denominator.

questions.title: No data
questions.prompt: Choose the one incorrect way to handle periods with no data points in the order API SLI.

choices.text: Distinguish between there being no requests and measurement having stopped.
choices.explanation: The two do not mean the same thing.

choices.text: Do not investigate because no data is always normal.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This could cause missing measurements to go unnoticed.

choices.text: Use traffic or a heartbeat to help interpret and check what no data means.
choices.explanation: This helps distinguish zero requests from measurement having stopped.

learning.reason: Do not replace missing data with success.
learning.concept: No data can have multiple meanings.

questions.title: SLOs and alerts
questions.prompt: Choose two correct statements about designing SLOs and alerts.

choices.text: Define a threshold, target, and observation window in the SLO.
choices.explanation: Clarify what must be achieved and by when.

choices.text: You can treat monthly and recent quality as equivalent even without defining an observation window.
choices.explanation: Calendar and rolling windows are interpreted differently.

choices.text: An alert does not need to enable action after the notification.
choices.explanation: Send notifications when people can take action.

choices.text: Define what missing data means and the follow-up steps after a notification.
choices.explanation: Avoid missing measurement interruptions and connect alerts to action.

choices.text: Build an SLO using only the number of successes, without a numerator and denominator.
choices.explanation: The scope cannot be made clear.

learning.reason: Connect measurement to action.
learning.concept: An SLO defines the window and target; an alert prompts action.

questions.title: Hypotheses
questions.prompt: Select the two incorrect ways of handling hypotheses during incident investigation.

choices.text: Fix the time, operation being investigated, user impact, and recent changes.
choices.explanation: This is the foundation for creating a basis for comparison.

choices.text: Treat a single correlation as proof of causation.
choices.explanation: That is incorrect. Use additional observations to support or refute the hypothesis.

choices.text: Form candidate causes from observations and how the system works.
choices.explanation: This is where a hypothesis starts.

choices.text: Compare candidates using traces, logs, and metrics.
choices.explanation: Test the hypothesis using other evidence.

choices.text: Ignore results that refute the hypothesis and accept only the first suspected cause.
choices.explanation: That is incorrect. Refuting evidence is a reason to reconsider the hypothesis.

learning.reason: Do not jump from observations to conclusions.
learning.concept: Make hypotheses falsifiable.

questions.title: Validating Configuration Changes
questions.prompt: Select two statements that are incorrect when checking for improvement before and after changing the connection pool settings.

choices.text: Conclude that user impact has improved if CPU alone goes down.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Compare user impact, such as errors and latency, under the same conditions as well.

choices.text: Compare the same SLI, time window, and target operation before and after the change.
choices.explanation: Keep the comparison conditions consistent.

choices.text: Also check for changes in traces that support the hypothesis of connection waits.
choices.explanation: Check for evidence supporting the hypothesis.

choices.text: Since a correlation is visible, change all high-impact environments at once.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Choose a test that limits the impact.

choices.text: Record unresolved questions and results for use in the next investigation.
choices.explanation: This makes the decision reproducible.

learning.reason: Evaluate changes based on user impact.
learning.concept: Compare before and after under the same conditions.

questions.title: Improvement conclusion
questions.prompt: Choose two statements that are incorrect ways to verify an improvement after HTTP 5xx errors and high CPU.

choices.text: Compare traffic, dependencies, and traces to narrow down possible causes.
choices.explanation: This provides additional evidence for testing correlations.

choices.text: After the change, check errors and latency for the same operation.
choices.explanation: This evaluates whether the impact on users has improved.

choices.text: Record CPU as the sole cause because CPU and 5xx errors rose at the same time.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Changes occurring at the same time alone do not establish causation.

choices.text: Test the hypothesis with a change that limits the impact.
choices.explanation: This can safely add to the evidence.

choices.text: Change the SLO observation window and directly compare the values before and after the change.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Improvement cannot be assessed unless the comparison uses the same window.

learning.reason: Verify causation and improvement through observation.
learning.concept: Evaluate under the same conditions.
